label: Mark 1:2
text: "Isaiah" is used loosely by Mark — the quotation actually blends Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, a common practice among Jewish teachers who let the more prominent passage govern the citation. "It is written" translates a perfect tense (gegraptai), meaning not just "was once written" but "stands written, and stands written still" — the record is permanent, on the books. "I send my messenger" uses apostellō, the verb behind our word "apostle": not a casual errand but a formal commission, an envoy sent with authority to act on the sender's behalf. His job, "prepare the way," draws on the language of advance men who leveled roads ahead of a king's procession. The Baptist's whole ministry was that — getting the road ready for someone greater walking behind him.
translation: As it stands written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send forth my messenger, on formal commission, before your face, who shall make ready your way.

label: Mark 1:3
text: "The voice" carries no definite article in the Greek — John is "a voice," not "the voice"; he points past himself to the greater One coming behind him. "Crying" (boáo) is the verb for an emotional, full-throated shout, distinct from a cooler word simply meaning "to call out" — the Baptist's preaching came from the heart and struck the heart. "Prepare" (hetoimázō) is aorist imperative, plural — a blunt, one-time command issued to the whole nation, with the clipped urgency of a military order and no room for delay. "Make his paths straight," by contrast, shifts to a present imperative — not a single act of welcome but a continuous, habitual readiness. "Straight" (euthús) describes the level, well-graded roads built for a king's procession; "paths" (tríbolos) is a worn trail, not a highway — the image is modest and personal, pointing to the ordinary business of a heart kept ready rather than one grand gesture. "Lord" appears without the article, throwing the weight onto quality rather than bare identity: a road fit for Jehovah himself.
translation: A voice of one crying: Make ready the road of the Lord; be continually making his paths straight.

label: Mark 1:4
text: "There arose" translates egeneto, the verb used elsewhere for something stepping onto the stage of history — not merely "John showed up," but "John's appearance marked an epoch." "Unto the remission of sins" is where most translations mislead. The preposition (eis) doesn't always carry the cause-and-effect sense English "unto" implies — elsewhere in the New Testament the same preposition means "because of." John's baptism didn't produce forgiveness; it testified to forgiveness already given. "Repentance" (metanoia) is literally a change of mind, not sorrow — the New Testament has a separate word for regret without change (used of Judas).
translation: John the baptizer stepped onto the scene in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of a change of mind, because sins had already been put away.

label: Mark 1:5
text: "There went out" renders an imperfect tense (ekporeuomai) — not a single mass movement but a steady, continuous stream, people arriving one after another over time. The preposition "unto" (pros) implies more than direction; it pictures people coming face to face with John, deliberately, each transacting personal business with the God he represented. "Baptized in the Jordan" uses en, not eis — "in," not "into" — picturing submersion in the river itself. "Confessing" is a present participle running alongside the main verb "baptized," meaning the confessing happened at the same moment as the baptizing — proof the repentance had already taken place before the rite, and baptism simply announced it publicly. The word for "confess" (homologeō) literally means "to say the same thing" — to agree with God's verdict on one's sin, not merely admit a fact about oneself.
translation: And there kept going out to him, to meet him face to face, all the country of Judea, and all they of Jerusalem, and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, agreeing with God about their sins even as they were baptized.

label: Mark 1:6
text: "Clothed" is a perfect participle — this was John's regular, habitual dress, not a costume assumed for effect. And "hair" is plural in the Greek: the garment was a coarse cloth woven from camel hairs, not a camel's hide draped over his shoulders. His diet of locusts and wild honey reflects the ordinary fare of a wilderness dweller living off what the desert supplied — honey gathered from wild bee colonies nesting in the limestone cliffs of Judea, a food source desert hunters in that region still relied on.
translation: Now John was habitually clothed in a garment woven of camel's hairs, with a leather belt about his waist; and he ate locusts and wild honey.

label: Mark 1:7
text: "There cometh one mightier than I" carries the definite article in Greek — not merely "someone," but "the One," a specific, expected figure. The sandal-thong detail is deliberate: untying a guest's sandals was the lowest task assigned to a household slave, and John places himself beneath even that — he won't claim the dignity of a servant in the presence of the One coming. That same self-effacement shows up later in his own words, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30): "must" translates dei, a term for what is necessary by the very nature of the situation. The forerunner recedes as the King advances — not so much an act of humility as the built-in shape of the relationship between herald and sovereign.
translation: And he kept proclaiming, saying, There comes after me the One who is mightier than I, the thong of whose sandals I am not fit to stoop down and untie.

label: Mark 1:8
text: John frames the contrast with emphatic pronouns — "as for myself" (egō) against "he himself" (autos) — sharpening the difference between his own baptism and the Messiah's. Both baptisms use the same preposition en ("in"), but the grammar shifts: John's is locative of place — a physical location, the Jordan River — while the Messiah's is locative of sphere, one idea confined within another rather than a location. John didn't apply water to people the way Jesus applies the Spirit to people; the parallel is baptism as immersion into a new realm, not substance poured on. What John announced here found its fulfillment at Pentecost, when the Spirit placed believers into the body of Christ.
translation: As for myself, I baptized you in water; but he himself shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit.

label: Mark 1:9
text: "In Jordan" translates eis — "into," a preposition of motion — while the next verse uses ek, "out from within." The picture is immersion: Jesus went down into the river and came back up out of it. He had no sin of his own to confess, yet he took his place among the repentant of Israel rather than standing apart from them — identifying with the people he had come to save before he ever began saving them.
translation: And it came to pass in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John into the Jordan.

label: Mark 1:10
text: "Opened" translates schízō — not a door swinging wide but heaven being torn or rent apart, a violent, decisive image. And the Spirit descends "into" him — eis, not the epi ("upon") one might expect — language suggesting the Spirit taking up residence within the Messiah rather than simply alighting on him for a moment. This was the anointing that equipped him for his threefold work as prophet, priest, and king.
translation: And immediately, coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens rent asunder, and the Spirit, as a dove, descending into him.

label: Mark 1:11
text: "From heaven" uses ek, not apo — "out from within," not merely "from the edge of." The voice comes from inside heaven itself, a place with real boundaries, capable of being opened and shut. "Thou art my beloved Son" places heavy emphasis on the pronoun "thou" (sú) — as for you, in contrast to everyone else. Elsewhere Jesus calls God his own Father using a word for what belongs to someone privately and uniquely, not shared sonship but singular sonship. "Beloved" is agapē, love called out by the sheer worth of what is loved — the Father's delight in the Son. That delight is stated in the aorist tense, gathering all of time into one unbroken whole: a pleasure with no beginning and no end, not a reaction to this one moment.
translation: And there came a voice out from within heaven: Thou art my Son, the beloved, in whom I was well pleased.

label: Mark 1:12
text: "Driveth him" is ekbállō — a forceful word, "to throw out from within, to drive out," the same verb Mark uses elsewhere for casting out demons. Matthew and Luke use gentler terms ("led up," "led"), but Mark's choice pictures something closer to compulsion than a leisurely walk — the Spirit thrusting Jesus into the wilderness under the weight of an intense, singular purpose, not reluctant obedience.
translation: And immediately the Spirit throws him forcibly out into the wilderness.

label: Mark 1:13
text:
"Tempted" is peirazomai, a word whose root sense is "to test, to probe for what's inside" — used first of examining someone to see what strength or weakness is really there, and only secondarily of soliciting someone toward evil. Both senses are active here: Satan is testing what stands ready in the Last Adam, and at the same time trying to talk him into sin. "Of Satan" uses hupo, marking personal agency — this was a real adversary, not an abstract force. The name "Satan" is a Hebrew word for adversary; "devil" (diabolos) comes from a verb meaning to slander or maliciously misrepresent — the accuser's business is distortion. "The angels ministered" — with the definite article, specific angels assigned to the task — uses an imperfect tense: not a single visit but continuous attendance through the whole forty days.

The proclamation that follows ("the time is fulfilled") uses a perfect passive verb — not simply "the time has arrived" but "the time has arrived, and that arrival still stands": the moment has come and remains epochal. "Time" here is kairos, a marked, appointed moment, not the ordinary ticking of chronos. And "gospel" (euaggelion) is simply "good news" — news that originates with God, not merely news about him.
translation:
And he was in the wilderness forty days, being put to the test by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts, and the angels were continually ministering to him.

The time stands fulfilled, and remains so, and the kingdom of God has drawn near: keep on changing your minds, and keep on believing in the good news.

label: Mark 1:16
text: "By the sea" is para, "alongside," used twice in the verse — a deliberately close, physical picture of Jesus walking right along the water's edge where the fishermen worked. "Casting a net" (amphibállō) combines the verb "to throw" with a word for "on both sides" — the practiced, back-and-forth motion of a net cast first one way, then another.
translation: And passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother casting a net on both sides, back and forth, in the sea; for they were fishermen.

label: Mark 1:17
text: "Come" (deute) is the same summons Jesus later uses to call Lazarus out of the tomb — an urgent, personal "come here." Paired with "after," it carries the sense of joining someone's company, not just walking behind them. "I will make you to become fishers of men" is telling in its phrasing — "make... become" points to a gradual process, not an instant transformation. Discipleship, from the first invitation, was framed as something that would take time.
translation: And Jesus said to them, Come here, join yourselves to me, and I will make you to become, by degrees, fishers of men.

label: Mark 1:18
text: "Forsook" (aphiēmi) carries a prefix implying separation — not simply setting the nets aside for the day but breaking away from that whole way of life — and the aorist tense marks it as a decisive, complete, one-time break, not a tentative pause. "Followed" (akoloutheō) literally means to walk the same road as someone, and it's used here with a case ending implying "following with" rather than "following behind": companionship, shared travel, not trailing at a distance.
translation: And straightway they broke away from their nets, once for all, and walked the same road with him.

label: Mark 1:19
text: "The ship" is ploion, the substantial fishing vessel, not the small tender boat sometimes towed behind it. "Mending" (katartízō) means restoring what's torn so it's ready for use again — ordinary maintenance, not repair after some disaster. And since a boat of that size would typically be moored some distance offshore, Jesus's call to James and John was likely shouted — the word for "called" carries that sense of calling out loudly — across open water.
translation: And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who also were in their boat, restoring their nets to order, and he called out to them at once, loudly, across the water.

label: Mark 1:20
text: "Went after him" is apēlthon, built on the same separating prefix as the previous verse's "forsook" — the word itself carries the idea of leaving one thing behind in the very act of going toward another.
translation: And immediately he called them; and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants, and went off, away from that life, after him.

label: Mark 1:21
text: "Synagogue" is built from a word for "going" plus "with" — literally, the place people gather by coming together. "Taught" uses an inchoative imperfect, a tense that marks the beginning of an ongoing action: the moment Jesus entered, he set into extended teaching, not a brief remark. Mark uses both kērussō ("to proclaim," the herald's public announcement) and didaskō ("to teach," patient instruction) of Jesus elsewhere — he suited his method to the moment, sometimes announcing, sometimes explaining.
translation: And they go into Capernaum; and immediately on the Sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, the gathering place, and set at once into teaching, and kept on teaching.

label: Mark 1:22
text:
"Astonished" (ekplēssō) is a violent word — to be struck out of one's composure, shocked to the edge of panic — and it's passive: something outside the crowd hit them and produced this reaction. The verb "he taught" is periphrastic, stretching the action out: "he was teaching," ongoing, not a single remark. "Authority" (exousia) is built on a root meaning "to be out of" — properly, delegated authority, power lent by someone else. The striking thing Mark records is that the crowd sensed Jesus speaking with authority that was his own, not borrowed the way the scribes borrowed the rulings of earlier rabbis.

What happened next confirmed it. Mark's phrase for the possessed man, "with an unclean spirit," is literally "in a spirit, an unclean one" — describing someone living within the grip and control of the presence inhabiting him. "He cried out" is a cry wrenched up from deep in the throat — visceral, not measured speech.
translation:
And they were struck clean out of their composure at his teaching: for he was continually teaching them as one having authority of his own, and not as the scribes, who taught on authority borrowed from others.

And there was in their synagogue a man in a spirit, an unclean one; and he cried out, a cry wrenched up from deep in the throat.

label: Mark 1:25
text: Greek has two words for "rebuke": one describes a correction that actually brings the offender to admit wrongdoing, the other (epitimaō, used here) simply silences without producing any acknowledgment of sin — fitting, since demons never repent. "Hold thy peace" is far blunter in the original: the verb means literally "to muzzle," the same word used of muzzling an ox — something closer to "shut your mouth" than the polished English suggests. Both verbs in the command are aorist imperative — sharp, immediate orders meant to be obeyed on the spot, with no room for delay.
translation: And Jesus rebuked him sharply, saying, Be muzzled, shut your mouth, and come out of him, at once.

label: Mark 1:26
text: "Had torn him" (sparassō) is a medical term for violent convulsion — the demon's parting shot, a fit of vindictiveness on the way out rather than any lingering struggle for control.
translation: And the unclean spirit, convulsing him violently and crying with a loud voice, came out of him.

label: Mark 1:27
text: Mark reaches for a second, distinct word for amazement here — thamébeō, blending astonishment with real fear, alongside the ekplēssō he used back in verse 22 — the crowd's reaction was deepening. "They questioned among themselves" ("to seek together") is present tense, picturing an animated, ongoing debate rather than a passing murmur. Their question about "new" doctrine uses kainos, not neos — Greek distinguishes newness in time (neos) from newness in kind or quality (kainos): this wasn't simply teaching nobody had heard before, but teaching of an entirely different character than what they were used to. "He commands" (epitássō) is military language, the term for drawing up troops in formation — the crowd's real shock wasn't the exorcism itself but that unclean spirits fell into line under his command like soldiers under orders.
translation: And they were all struck with astonishment and dread, so that they kept on debating together among themselves, saying, What is this? A teaching, new in kind! For with authority he gives command even to the unclean spirits, and they fall into line under him.

label: Mark 1:28
text: "Fame" (akoē) is simply "the thing heard" — a report, the same word elsewhere translated "rumor." Word of him spread the ordinary way news spreads, by mouth, and it simply moved fast.
translation: And the report of him went out immediately everywhere into all the surrounding region of Galilee.

label: Mark 1:29
text: Mark's brief aside — that Peter was married, his mother-in-law living in his household, and that Jesus made this home his base in Capernaum — sets the domestic scene for the healing that follows. It's a small window into how ordinary and rooted in family life the disciples' world remained even after they left their nets.
translation: And immediately, coming out of the synagogue, they went into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.

label: Mark 1:30
text: "Lay sick" (katakeimai) is colloquial for being laid up, bedridden — and the imperfect tense means she'd been down for some time already, not freshly taken ill. "Of a fever" uses a present participle built on the Greek word for fire — she was, quite literally, burning. Luke, the physician among the gospel writers, adds his own diagnostic touch, describing Jesus as standing over her the way a doctor examines a patient.
translation: Now Simon's mother-in-law was lying there, having been sick of a fever for some time, continually burning; and at once they tell him about her.

label: Mark 1:31
text:
"He came" (proselyōn) carries a prefix meaning "facing" — Jesus approached and stood facing her, the same posture Luke describes as a physician bending over a patient. "Took her by the hand and lifted her up" reads in the Greek order as "he lifted her up, having taken her hand" — the grasp preceding and enabling the lift. "She ministered unto them" is imperfect, picturing ongoing service rather than one clean gesture — there was a meal to prepare, and she set about doing it.

That evening, once the sun had "gone under" (the same verb used for the sun sinking into the sea) and the Sabbath had ended, people carried their sick to the door in a steady stream — "brought" is imperfect, continuous traffic rather than a single crowd arriving at once. "Gathered together" is a perfect participle: the crowd had assembled and settled in, camped at the door, waiting until their business was finished.
translation:
And he came and stood facing her, and, having taken hold of her hand, lifted her up; and the fever left her, and she set about serving them, continually.

And at evening, when the sun had gone down under, they kept bringing to him all who were sick and those under the power of demons, in a steady stream. And the whole city was gathered together, and stood camped, at the door.

label: Mark 1:34
text: "Divers diseases" translates poikilos, "variegated" — every different kind. "Suffered [them] not to speak" is imperfect, describing an ongoing, repeated refusal rather than one command — the demons kept trying, and Jesus kept silencing them, precisely because they recognized who he was and he had no use for that kind of testimony.
translation: And he healed many who were sick with diseases of every different kind, and cast out many demons; and he kept on not permitting the demons to speak, because they kept on knowing him.

label: Mark 1:35
text: "In the morning" marks the last watch of the night, roughly three to six a.m., and "a great while before day" narrows it further — still dark, early in that watch. "Prayed" (proseuchomai) adds a prefix meaning "toward" to the ordinary word for prayer, sharpening it into consciously directed address to God rather than vague devotion — and the imperfect tense pictures him praying on through those early hours, not offering a brief word and rising.
translation: And rising up very early, while it was yet dark, in the last watch of the night, he went out and departed into a desert place, and there he kept on praying, directing himself toward the Father.

label: Mark 1:36
text: "Followed after him" is katadiōkō, a hunting term — the prefix adds the sense of pursuit carried through to its conclusion. Peter and the others didn't casually go looking for Jesus; they tracked him down.
translation: And Simon and those who were with him hunted him down, tracking him to the end.

label: Mark 1:37
text: "All men seek for thee" uses a present tense verb — everyone is seeking, right now, an ongoing search rather than a single inquiry. "All" is the disciples' own hyperbole, but it captures something real: demand for him had already outrun the town.
translation: And when they found him, they said to him, Everyone is continually searching for you, right now.

label: Mark 1:38
text: "Let us go" (agōmen) is a present hortatory subjunctive — "let us keep going," a sustained journey rather than one trip. "Next towns" means unwalled country towns, modest places, not larger walled cities. "I came forth" points back to why he left Capernaum in the first place — the purpose was never to settle in one town but to keep moving outward.
translation: And he says to them, Let us keep going on into the neighboring country towns, that I may keep proclaiming there also; for it was for this purpose I came forth.

label: Mark 1:39
text: "He came" opens the verse in the Greek text but goes untranslated in older English versions — a small reminder that Mark tracks Jesus's continuous movement from town to town, carrying forward the resolve just voiced in the previous verse.
translation: And he kept coming, preaching in their synagogues throughout all Galilee, and casting out the demons.

label: Mark 1:40
text: "There came" is a historic present, lending a past event the immediacy of something happening right now before the reader. "To him" again pictures a face-to-face confrontation, not a passing encounter. "Beseeching" (parakaleō) is an urgent plea — "please, I beg you." And Greek has two words for "willing": one rooted in reason, the other in feeling. The leper uses the emotional one — he isn't appealing to Jesus's logic but to his heart.
translation: And there comes to him a leper, face to face, pleading with him, and kneeling down to him, and saying to him, If you are willing, from your heart, you are able to make me clean.

label: Mark 1:41
text: "Moved with compassion" (splagchnizomai) is a gut-level word for pity, compassion felt in the body, not merely decided upon — Mark's eye for Jesus's inner life shows here. The sequence in the Greek matters: the decision to heal and the healing itself both preceded the touch and the words — Jesus touched the leper not in order to cleanse him, but to demonstrate to onlookers that he already had, since Jewish law forbade touching a leper and Jesus, who kept the law, would not have touched him while he remained unclean. "Be thou clean" is aorist passive imperative — a command for something to happen immediately and completely, not by degrees.
translation: And, moved with compassion in the depths of his being, he stretched forth his hand and touched him, and says to him, I am willing; be made clean, at once and completely.

label: Mark 1:42
text: "The leprosy departed" carries the same separating prefix seen elsewhere in Mark — a complete, clean break between the man and his disease, nothing left behind. Jesus's charge that follows is unusually forceful — the verb originally described the snort of a horse, and in this context conveys stern, forceful insistence rather than literal anger. The urgency makes sense: an uncontrolled report before the priest had officially certified the cure risked provoking hostile scrutiny before the healing could even be verified through the proper channels — so Jesus pushed him out and toward the one authority who could make the cleansing official.
translation: And immediately the leprosy went off from him, completely, and he was made clean.

label: Mark 1:45
text: "To publish" and "to blaze abroad" are both continuous in force — the man didn't make one announcement but kept proclaiming, kept spreading the story, until Jesus could no longer enter a town openly. "Came" is imperfect too: people kept arriving, from everywhere, in an unbroken stream.
translation: But he went out and began to keep proclaiming it freely, and to keep spreading the matter abroad, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter into a city, but was without, in desert places; and they kept coming to him from every quarter, in an unbroken stream.

label: Mark 2:2
text: The house could not hold the crowd, and Mark says there was no longer room even at the door (using a construction, hōste, that means "so much so that") — the picture is of the crowd overflowing the threshold itself. For "preached" Mark chooses laleō rather than kērussō, the word for a formal, authoritative public proclamation. Laleō is the everyday word for conversational speech — used elsewhere of birds chattering and children prattling — and its use here suggests Jesus talking with this crowd rather than orating at them, an intimate, unhurried address rather than a formal sermon. The verb is imperfect: not a single burst of speech but an ongoing conversation, He kept on talking to them.
translation: And many were gathered together, so that there was no longer room, no, not even near the door; and he kept on talking with them, ordinary and unhurried, the word.

label: Mark 2:3
text: Mark switches into the present tense to narrate this past event — "they come" rather than "they came" — the same device we use telling a story today for dramatic immediacy: you can watch it happening. The word behind "sick of the palsy," paralutikos, is built from a root meaning "to loosen" plus "alongside" — literally a slackening of the nerves along one side of the body, which is exactly our English "paralytic." "Borne of four" uses a participle from airō, "to lift up and carry what has been lifted" — the man is described as someone raised up and held aloft by the four men rather than merely accompanied by them, emphasizing his complete helplessness and their labor.
translation: And they come, bringing to him a paralyzed man, lifted up and carried by four men.

label: Mark 2:4
text: "They uncovered the roof" translates a cognate construction in Greek — literally "they unroofed the roof," a rare verb that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. This wasn't shingles lifted off; a flat oriental roof of that era was packed mortar, tar, ash, and sand over cross-laid timbers or stone slabs, so the verb for "broken up" means to dig or scoop out — real excavation, not a quick patch removed. "Let down" pictures ropes lowering the pallet from that opening to the floor below, and the word for the paralytic's condition as he "lay" there is the same verb used of someone bedridden — he was dead weight, wholly dependent on the four men's effort to get him into the room at all.
translation: And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they unroofed the roof where he was; and having dug it out, they let down the pallet on which the paralyzed man lay, dead weight.

label: Mark 2:5
text:
"Their faith" is significant — the pronoun points back to the four men and whoever else tore open that roof, not necessarily to the paralytic himself. Their determined, dirty, expensive labor was the outward proof of an inward trust; Jesus reads the effort as the evidence. He addresses the man as "child" (teknon) rather than the more formal "son" (huios) — a warm, familiar term of address used even toward grown men in everyday Greek of the period, not baby talk but affection. "Be forgiven" is a present-tense verb stating a settled fact, better rendered "your sins are put away" — not a wish or a future promise but a pronouncement of something already accomplished. The verb itself, aphiēmi, has the root sense of releasing or sending off; it's the word used elsewhere for cancelling a debt outright — an obligation simply let go, no longer held against the debtor.

The scribes' silent objection is described with dialogizomai, "to weigh and turn over in the mind" — a private, wordless calculation, though evidently visible enough on their faces that Jesus reads it instantly. Their charge, "he is blaspheming," uses a verb meaning to speak in a way that injures or slanders — in their theology, entirely correct reasoning, since only God can cancel sin. Their logic was sound; what they'd missed was who stood in front of them.
translation:
And Jesus, seeing their faith, the faith of those who carried him, says to the paralyzed man, Child, your sins are, here and now, put away, cancelled like a debt released.

But there were certain of the scribes sitting there, weighing it over in their hearts, silently: Why does this man speak thus? He injures God with slanderous speech: who is able to put away sins but God alone?

label: Mark 2:8
text: "Perceived" translates a compound built on the verb for experiential knowing, sharpened by a prefix that adds the sense of "fully" or "thoroughly" — Jesus doesn't merely sense something is wrong, He is instantly and completely aware of exactly what the scribes are thinking. "In his spirit" points to the inner faculty of thought, will, and feeling — the seat of reasoning itself — so the picture is of Jesus reading their unspoken deliberation directly, without anyone having said a word.
translation: And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit, fully and at once, that they were reasoning thus within themselves, says to them, Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?

label: Mark 2:9
text:
The command to the paralytic stacks up three imperatives with different force. "Arise" is present tense, "be arising" — get up and keep getting up, a process. "Take up your bed" is aorist, snapped out with military curtness — a single decisive action, done at once. "Walk" is present again — start walking and keep walking, not a single test step but a standing ability restored for good.

Jesus explains the healing was proof of "authority" — exousia, not the word for raw power (dunamis) but for delegated right to act, the authority a person has when someone else has commissioned them to act in his name. The Son of Man exercises on earth an authority that belongs properly to God the Father who sent Him — which is exactly the scribes' own logic turned back on them: if only God forgives sins, and this man visibly holds that authority, their objection answers itself. "Go your way" uses a verb for a decisive parting — the word used of someone ending their attendance on another and departing for good — hinting that Jesus wanted the healed man to slip quietly home rather than linger and draw a crowd that would only inflame the opposition further.
translation: Which is easier, to say to the paralyzed man, Your sins are put away; or to say, Keep on arising, take up your pallet at once, and keep on walking? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority, delegated to him, on earth to put away sins, he says to the paralyzed man, I say to you, keep on arising, take up your pallet, at once, and go off to your own home, for good.

label: Mark 2:12
text: "They were amazed" uses the verb behind our English word "ecstasy" — literally "to stand outside oneself." It describes a state so overtaken by wonder that ordinary awareness shuts down; for a moment the crowd's whole attention is swallowed by what they've just watched, as though they'd stepped outside their own routine perception of the world. That's the intensity Mark is reaching for — not polite surprise but people momentarily beside themselves.
translation: And immediately he arose, took up the pallet, and went out before them all, so that they were all put outside of themselves, standing beside themselves in wonder, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it in this fashion.

label: Mark 2:13
text: "By the seaside" uses a preposition meaning "alongside," suggesting Jesus wasn't just heading to the shore but walking its length — a stretch of quiet, moving water and open air that a fully human Messiah, worn from constant demand, would have found restorative. Both verbs describing the crowd and His teaching are imperfect: the people kept coming, and He kept right on teaching them — an ongoing scene, not a single event.
translation: And he went out again alongside the sea, walking its length; and all the crowd kept coming to him, and he kept on teaching them.

label: Mark 2:14
text: Levi was seated at the customs post on the Capernaum road, the crossing point for traffic and shipping on the Sea of Galilee — a job that made him wealthy and despised in equal measure, a Jew collecting Roman tax from fellow Jews. "Follow" (akoloutheō) is built on the idea of walking the same road as another, joining him as a companion and a disciple, and Jesus gives it as a command, not a suggestion — present tense, meaning "start now and keep doing it as a way of life." The pronoun rendered "me" is in a case that signals accompaniment rather than mere pursuit: this isn't "follow behind me" but "walk this road with me," side by side rather than trailing single file. Levi got up and did exactly that — leaving a lucrative desk for an itinerant teacher, on nothing more than the force of that call.
translation: And passing by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office, and says to him, Start following, and keep on walking this road with me. And he arose and walked the road with him.

label: Mark 2:15
text: "Sat at meat" translates the ordinary word for reclining — the posture of the meal itself, since diners in that culture lay along low couches around the table rather than sitting in chairs. The word rendered "meat" simply means food in general, not animal flesh specifically — the same word Jesus uses later of His true nourishment, "to do the will of him that sent me." "Disciples" (mathētēs) is simply "one who learns" — a description of a following, not a guarantee of salvation; the word covers everyone attached to Jesus as a student, faithful or not, which is worth remembering given how the story of one particular disciple among the Twelve ends.
translation: And it came to pass, as he reclined at table in his house, that many tax collectors and sinners were reclining together with Jesus and his learners: for there were many, and they were following him.

label: Mark 2:16
text: The best manuscripts read "the scribes of the Pharisees" rather than "the scribes and the Pharisees" — meaning specifically the scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party, essentially trained legal specialists attached to that particular school of thought. Their scandal wasn't abstract: reclining at a meal in that culture was a statement of fellowship and acceptance, so for Jesus to share a couch with tax collectors was, in their eyes, to identify with them.
translation: And when the scribes who belonged to the Pharisees saw that he was eating together, in fellowship, with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his learners, Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?

label: Mark 2:17
text: "Whole" translates a word meaning simply "strong," and "sick" repeats the word Mark already used back in 1:32 for the diseased crowds brought to Jesus at evening — literally "those having it badly." The Greek word order puts the emphasis exactly where Jesus wants it: no need have the strong of a doctor, but the sick. That's His answer for being found at Levi's table among tax collectors — not that He enjoyed the company of open sin, but that a doctor's place is with the ill, not the well.
translation: And hearing it, Jesus says to them, Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who have it badly. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

label: Mark 2:18
text: "Used to fast" is a periphrastic imperfect construction, stressing that John's disciples and the Pharisees were in the middle of observing a fast at that very moment, not merely that fasting was their general habit. There's an irony buried here: John himself had called the Pharisees a brood of vipers, yet his own disciples are now standing shoulder to shoulder with them, using shared ritual observance to needle Jesus over a table He shared with sinners.
translation: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were, at that very time, in the midst of fasting; and they come and say to him, Why do John's disciples and the Pharisees' disciples fast, but your disciples do not fast?

label: Mark 2:19
text: "Children of the bridechamber" is literally "sons" — not the groomsmen but the invited wedding guests, since Galilee didn't follow the Judean custom of formal groomsmen. Jesus is reaching back to John the Baptist's own image of himself as "friend of the bridegroom" and recasting it — He is the bridegroom, and mourning has no place at a wedding feast while the groom is present. The question is framed with a negative particle that signals Jesus already expects the answer "no" — He isn't wondering aloud, He's stating the obvious and daring anyone to disagree.
translation: And Jesus said to them, The sons of the bridechamber cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, can they? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they are not able to fast.

label: Mark 2:20
text: "The days will come" has no article on "days" in the Greek — the stress falls on quality, not a calendar date: days of a certain grim character are coming. The word order puts "taken away" first for emphasis, and the reference is to the cross. The better manuscripts then shift from plural "days" to a solitary "in that day" — a single, weighted moment rather than a stretch of time, marking the crucifixion off as uniquely severe.
translation: But days shall come, days of a certain grim character, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, wrenched away, and then, in that day, they shall fast.

label: Mark 2:21
text: "New cloth" is agnaphos, "unfulled" — cloth that hasn't yet gone through the fuller's process of washing, shrinking, and pressing that stabilizes it. Sewn onto a worn garment, it will still shrink after the fact and tear the weakened fabric around it. And "old" here isn't the word for old in time (archaios) but for old through use — worn out, threadbare, no longer able to hold a strong new patch. The image fits the larger point: Jesus's message isn't a repair grafted onto the old system, it's something new that the old system cannot contain without tearing further.
translation: No man sews a patch of unfulled cloth on a garment worn threadbare through use: else the new piece that fills it up takes away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made.

label: Mark 2:22
text: "Bottles" misleads modern ears — these are wineskins, made of animal hide, which can burst under the pressure of fermenting wine in a way glass containers with a cork wouldn't. Two different words for "new" appear: the wine is neos, new in time, freshly made; the skins needed are kainos, new in kind or condition, not previously stretched and dried out. Put fresh wine in a wineskin already worn stiff with age (palaios again) and the pressure of fermentation splits it — both wine and skin are ruined. It's the same lesson as the patch: grace poured into the old container of the law destroys both.
translation: And no man puts new wine, fresh-made, into skins grown old and stiff with use: else the wine bursts the skins, and the wine is spilled out, and the skins are destroyed: but new wine must go into skins new in condition.

label: Mark 2:23
text: "Went through the cornfields" pictures Jesus and His disciples on a footpath cutting alongside and through standing grain — the verb combines both ideas, journeying along the edge and through the field itself. "Ears of corn" is misleading to modern readers: the Greek word means simply a head of grain, wheat or barley, and "corn" here is just old English usage for grain generally, the way the King James also renders "a grain of wheat" with the same word. His disciples are picking heads of grain by hand as they walk, satisfying hunger on the move, nothing more.
translation: And it came to pass that he went, on a Sabbath day, along the path and through the standing grain; and his disciples began, as they went, to pick the heads of grain by hand.

label: Mark 2:24
text: "The Pharisees said" uses an imperfect verb, not the simple aorist Mark could have chosen if he only meant to report a single remark — the tense signals they kept pressing the point, repeating the accusation. And notice the shift: earlier they complained to His disciples about His table company; now they address Jesus directly, treating the disciples' hand-picked grain as reaping in miniature, and therefore a Sabbath violation.
translation: And the Pharisees kept saying to him, See, why are they doing on the Sabbath day that which is not lawful?

label: Mark 2:25
text: "Have you never read" expects the answer "yes" — Jesus isn't testing their Bible knowledge, He's reminding scholars of the law of something they already know cold, and turning it back on them. The verbs throughout stay singular, keeping David alone in the spotlight as the one who acted, with his companions mentioned only as an afterthought — which sharpens the parallel Jesus is drawing: a recognized, God-approved leader broke a ceremonial rule under pressing need, and no one condemned him for it.
translation: And he says to them, Have you never read what David did, when he had need and was hungry, he and those who were with him?

label: Mark 2:26
text: "House of God" here means the tabernacle, since the temple didn't yet exist in David's day. "Shewbread" translates a phrase built from "before" and "to set" — literally "the loaves of the setting-forth," bread set out before the Lord, which the Jews themselves called "the bread of the face," meaning God's presence. Twelve loaves were baked and set on the table each week, normally reserved for the priests alone to eat once replaced — which is precisely why the incident makes Jesus's point: even bread hedged around by ceremonial restriction gave way to human need.
translation: How he entered into the house of God, in the days of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the loaves of the setting-forth, the bread of the presence, which it is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?

label: Mark 2:27
text: "Man" translates anthrōpos, the generic word for humankind, not a term limited to males — the Sabbath exists for the sake of people in general. "Was made" is literally "came into existence," making the Sabbath a created means to a human end, not an end in itself — exactly the inversion the rabbinic tradition had made of it, treating people as existing to serve the day rather than the other way around. The verb for "he said" is imperfect too: this wasn't a point made once and dropped, but pressed home repeatedly against minds trained to think ceremonially.
translation: And he kept saying to them, again and again, The Sabbath came into existence for the sake of man, and not man for the sake of the Sabbath.

label: Mark 2:28
text: "Lord" (kurios) is the word for an owner, someone who possesses and controls a thing outright — but it's also the word the Greek Old Testament uses to render the divine name itself, carrying real overtones of deity here, not just authority over a ritual observance. Mark alone preserves a small word in this saying, better translated "even" than "also": the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath — striking precisely because the Sabbath was the one institution the formalists treated as untouchable, the last thing they'd have conceded belonged to Him.
translation: So that the Son of Man is Lord, owner and master, even of the Sabbath.

label: Mark 3:2
text: "They watched him" translates an imperfect tense — not a single glance but a stakeout, the Pharisees keeping our Lord under continuous surveillance to catch him healing on the Sabbath. The verb carries a prefixed preposition meaning "beside," picturing them as side-line observers who wanted no part of him yet couldn't look away — close enough to catch him in the act, careful to stay uninvolved. "That they might accuse him" uses the formal legal term for bringing a charge before a tribunal, not casual criticism. This was never curiosity. It was evidence-gathering for a prosecution already decided on.
translation: And they kept him under continuous watch, from the side, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath day, that they might bring a formal charge against him.

label: Mark 3:3
text: The command is more vivid in the Greek than the English lets on — literally "arise into the midst," step out where everyone can see you. Jesus doesn't quietly heal the man off to the side. He calls him into the center of the room, in full view of the very men watching for a violation, and forces the confrontation into the open before he does anything at all.
translation: And he says to the man who had the withered hand, Arise, and stand out here, in the midst, where all can see.

label: Mark 3:4
text: Jesus reframes the whole question before answering it. The Pharisees were thinking in terms of the letter of Sabbath law — is this technically permitted? Jesus asks instead whether it is lawful "to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill" — a category shift from legal compliance to plain ethics. For him there was no third option: refusing to do the good you're able to do is itself a form of doing harm. "They held their peace" is imperfect tense too — not a single silence but a held, deepening quiet. They had no answer, because his question wasn't playing by their rules.
translation: And he says to them, Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? But they kept on holding their peace, in a deepening, unbroken silence.

label: Mark 3:5
text: Mark pairs two different tenses on purpose. "He looked round about on them with anger" is aorist — one swift, sweeping glance, the prefixed preposition indicating it took in the whole circle of onlookers at once. "Being grieved" is present tense, durative — a grief that lingered under the anger and outlasted it. Greek actually has three separate words for anger, and Mark reaches for the one denoting a settled, principled response rather than either a passing flare-up or a forbidden, embittered exasperation — anger with an object and a cause, not mere temper. "Hardness" translates a word built from the noun for a callus: a heart that has grown a thick, insensible skin over it. The word for "heart" is singular in the Greek even though many men are in view, as though the whole company shared one hardened heart between them. "Restored" means literally brought back to its former condition — the hand made exactly as it had been.
translation: And when he had looked around on them all, in one sweeping glance, with anger, being grieved continually at the callused hardness of their heart, he says to the man, Stretch out your hand. And he stretched it out, and his hand was restored, exactly as it had been.

label: Mark 3:6
text: The alliance in this verse is the real shock. Pharisees and Herodians had nothing in common and ordinarily despised each other — the Pharisees zealous for the law and impatient with Rome, the Herodians attached to a dynasty that owed its throne to Roman favor and wasn't even properly Jewish by descent. Common hostility to Jesus did what nothing else could: it put them in the same room, plotting together. And it happened immediately — the text has them going straight from watching him heal to conspiring to kill him, on the same Sabbath.
translation: And the Pharisees went out, and immediately took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

label: Mark 3:7
text: "A great multitude" places the word for "great" in an emphatic position in the Greek — this was a crowd out of the ordinary even for Jesus. He withdraws toward open water, which makes practical sense: a lake shore gives room to retreat and a clear line back to a boat if the press of people becomes dangerous, which is exactly the problem the next few verses describe.
translation: But Jesus withdrew with his disciples toward the sea; and a great multitude, out of the ordinary even for him, followed from Galilee.

label: Mark 3:8
text: "What great things he did" is present tense in the Greek, not simple past — people were continually hearing reports of what he was doing, in real time, as the news kept spreading faster than he could travel. The crowd gathering from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, and beyond the Jordan wasn't responding to old news; it was chasing a story still unfolding.
translation: And from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and beyond Jordan, and around Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, hearing continually what great things he was doing, came to him.

label: Mark 3:9
text: Mark is precise about the boat. The word here is for a small rowboat, distinct from the larger fishing vessel used elsewhere — the dinghy that would normally be towed behind the bigger craft. "Wait on" translates a verb meaning to stand in constant readiness, and it's in a tense implying continuous action: the disciples kept a small boat rowing along just offshore the whole time, ready to pull Jesus out at a moment's notice. "Throng" is the same verb used elsewhere for pressing grapes to extract their juice — not mere crowding but a press capable of crushing a man. The precaution was not excessive.
translation: And he told his disciples that a small boat should stand in constant readiness for him because of the crowd, lest they press upon him, crushing him like grapes at the press.

label: Mark 3:10
text: The verb behind "pressed upon" means literally to fall upon or collide with — people weren't just crowding close, they were stumbling and shoving into him bodily in their eagerness to get near enough to touch him, hoping healing might come even through an accidental brush. "Plagues" translates a word that elsewhere means a stroke or a scourge — the same image behind our own phrase "a paralytic stroke." It's vivid, physical language for affliction, not a clinical term.
translation: For he had healed many, so that as many as had scourges, physical strokes of affliction, kept falling upon him, colliding with him bodily, to touch him.

label: Mark 3:11
text: Greek has two verbs for "to see," and Mark chooses the one used of a purposeful, evaluating look rather than a casual glance — the word you'd use of an officer inspecting troops, not a bystander watching a parade pass by. The unclean spirits recognized Jesus with informed, critical scrutiny, not vague unease. Both "fell down" and "cried out" are imperfect tense — repeated, ongoing action every time this happened, not a single incident. And the declaration "Thou art the Son of God" carries an intensive pronoun in the Greek that has no exact English equivalent but lands like "As for you — you are the Son of God," singling him out as utterly unique, in a class of his own. The demons knew exactly who they were dealing with.
translation: And whenever the unclean spirits, inspecting him with a scrutinizing look, saw him, they kept falling down before him, and kept crying out, saying, As for you, you are the Son of God.

label: Mark 3:12
text: "Straightly charged" translates a verb meaning to rebuke sharply, carrying in the background of its usage a sense of a penalty attached to disobedience — not a mild request but a forceful, binding order. Jesus refused the demons' testimony to his identity. However true their words were, he wanted no endorsement from that source; the truth about him was not going to be established by Satan's own subjects.
translation: And he kept sternly ordering them, under binding threat, that they should not make him known.

label: Mark 3:13–15
text:
"Calleth unto him" is in the middle voice, a form that in Greek marks the subject as acting in his own interest — Jesus called these men for himself, to belong to him. The verb for "would" carries its own intensive pronoun as well: "whom he himself desired." No one volunteered; he did the choosing, deliberately and alone. The men "went off" to him — the verb implies leaving something behind, stepping away from the crowd below to follow him up the mountain.

The purpose clauses that follow are worth noticing for their order: first "that they should be with him," a present tense implying ongoing, continuous fellowship — companionship before commission — and only then that he might send them out. "Send them forth" is the verb behind our word "apostle": to dispatch someone with credentials, as an authorized representative empowered to act on the sender's behalf. "Power to heal sicknesses and cast out devils" is not the word for God's own inherent supernatural power but a different term meaning delegated authority — the Twelve weren't given power in themselves, but were authorized to speak and act in Christ's name while the power remained his.
translation: And he goes up into the mountain, and calls to himself, for his own, those whom he himself desired; and they went off, away from the crowd below, to him. And he appointed twelve, that they might be continually with him, and that he might send them forth as his authorized representatives, to keep on proclaiming, and to have authority, delegated, not their own, to heal sicknesses, and to cast out demons.

label: Mark 3:16
text: "Surnamed" translates a verb meaning literally to place a name upon someone, in addition to what they already had. The name Peter comes from a Greek word for a detached, freestanding stone or fragment — distinct from the related feminine word for a massive bedrock ledge. The distinction matters: Simon is given the name of a solid, weighty stone, descriptive of the rock-like steadiness his character would grow into once transformed, not a description of what he already was. Impulsive, unpredictable Simon becomes, by name and by calling, Peter the rock.
translation: And upon Simon he placed the name Peter, a detached stone, a freestanding fragment, the man he would grow to become.

label: Mark 3:17
text: "Boanerges" is transliterated straight from a Semitic phrase meaning "sons of thunder." "Sons of" is a common Hebrew idiom in which a defining trait is spoken of as though it were a parent — a "son of thunder" is simply a thunderous man. The name fits what we know of James and John elsewhere: it was these two who wanted to call down fire on an inhospitable village. A nickname, not a formal title, but an apt one.
translation: And upon James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James, he placed the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder, men of a thunderous nature.

label: Mark 3:18
text: The names in this list carry their own small stories. Andrew is a Greek name built on the word for "man" and means simply "manly." Philip, also Greek, means "fond of horses." Matthew is Hebrew for "gift of God." Thomas means "twin." And Simon "the Canaanite" is better rendered "the Zealot" — a member of the fiercely nationalist, anti-Roman party of the day. Putting a Zealot and a Roman tax collector like Matthew in the same band of twelve says something about what following Jesus was already doing to old loyalties and old enemies.
translation: And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot.

label: Mark 3:19
text: "Iscariot" most likely means "man of Kerioth," naming Judas's hometown rather than any trait of his — a town in Judah near the border of Edom, according to Joshua's record. "Betrayed" translates a compound verb built from "to give" and a prefix meaning "alongside" — literally, to hand someone over. It's ordinary transactional language, the same word used elsewhere for handing over a prisoner or a piece of property, which is precisely the horror of it here.
translation: And Judas Iscariot, the man of Kerioth, who also handed him over, as one hands over a piece of property.

label: Mark 3:20
text: The crowd, which had presumably thinned while Jesus was up the mountain choosing the Twelve, reassembles the moment he comes back down — Mark implies enough time had passed for people to disperse and then regather, which tells us how determined they were not to miss him. The pressure was such that Jesus and his own household couldn't even manage a meal in peace.
translation: And the crowd comes together again, so that they were not even able to eat bread.

label: Mark 3:21
text: "His friends" is a misleading translation. The Greek phrase means literally "those from his side" — his own household, his family, not friends in the ordinary sense. That the same group is identified as his mother and brothers a few verses later confirms it. "He is beside himself" translates a verb meaning to be displaced from one's normal state of mind, used elsewhere of being driven out of one's senses entirely. His own family, alarmed by the scale of what they were hearing about his ministry, concluded he had lost his grip and set out to bring him home by force.
translation: And when those of his own household heard of it, they went out to lay hold of him: for they kept saying, He is displaced from his right mind, out of himself.

label: Mark 3:22
text: The scribes' accusation goes further than a mere alliance with evil. "He hath Beelzebub" implies possession — that the prince of demons is using Jesus as his own instrument, not merely cooperating with him. "Prince" translates a word meaning simply "first" or "ruler," the one holding chief place among the demons — a title of rank, not nobility. It's a calculated accusation: rather than deny the miracles, which were plainly happening, the scribes tried to reassign their source, crediting Satan instead of God in order to discredit Jesus's claim to be sent from God.
translation: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem kept saying, He has Beelzebub within him as his master, and, By the ruler of the demons he casts out demons.

label: Mark 3:23
text: The word for "parable" is built from a verb meaning "to throw alongside" — an illustration laid beside a truth so its shape becomes visible by comparison. "How can Satan cast out Satan" uses a Greek word for "how" that carries the force of "how is this even possible" — not a real question but the setup for a logical demonstration. Jesus meets their accusation on its own terms and shows it collapses under its own logic: casting out spirits by the aid of a stronger spirit requires a motive, and no ruler works to dismantle his own kingdom.
translation: And calling them to him, he began speaking to them in illustrations laid alongside the truth: How is it even possible for Satan to cast out Satan?

label: Mark 3:24–26
text: Jesus builds his case in three steps, each one an ordinary observation about how the world works before he applies it to Satan: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, a household divided against itself cannot stand, and therefore — the same must be true of Satan's kingdom, if the accusation against Jesus were true. No agent, human or spiritual, works to bring about his own collapse. The logic isn't Jesus defending himself so much as exposing the accusation as self-refuting.
translation: And if a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom is not able to stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he is not able to stand, but has an end.

label: Mark 3:27
text: "Spoil" translates a verb meaning to plunder thoroughly, to ransack completely, and the word behind "goods" refers to equipment or tools of a trade rather than mere possessions in general — the very apparatus a strong man depends on for his work. The image is precise: the demons are Satan's tools, and no one raids a strong man's house and strips his equipment from him unless the strong man himself has first been bound. Jesus's exorcisms are proof that the stronger man has already arrived.
translation: But no one is able to enter into the strong man's house and plunder thoroughly his equipment, unless he first binds the strong man; and then he will ransack his house completely.

label: Mark 3:28–30
text: "Blaspheme" is a transliterated Greek word meaning deliberate, malicious misrepresentation — reproachful speech aimed at discrediting someone, spoken knowing better. That's the precise charge here: the scribes knew the power at work in Jesus's miracles was not evil, and chose anyway to call it Satan's, in order to blunt its force as evidence. "Eternal damnation" is a genuinely poor rendering, resting on a corrupted Greek text that read "judgment" where the better manuscripts read "sin." The phrase actually means an eternal — or better, an everlasting — sin: not a sin that repeats itself endlessly, but one whose guilt, once incurred in full knowledge and defiance of the truth, is never lifted. It is the deliberate, informed nature of the misrepresentation that makes it what it is, not the category of sin itself.
translation: Truly I say to you, all their sins shall be forgiven the sons of men, and their deliberate, malicious misrepresentations of the truth, however many they utter; but whoever deliberately misrepresents, in full knowledge, the Holy Spirit, has never forgiveness, but is guilty of a sin that goes on forever, its guilt never lifted.

label: Mark 3:31
text: Mark switches into present tense here — "there come his mother and his brethren" — the kind of vivid present he uses to make a past event feel like it's unfolding as you read it. They stand outside rather than pushing in, and send word through the crowd rather than approaching directly, which suggests some hesitance about how to carry out what they'd come to do.
translation: And there come his mother and his brothers; and standing outside, they sent word in to him, calling him.

label: Mark 3:32
text: "Sat about him" pictures the crowd seated in a full circle surrounding Jesus, with the message about his family passed inward through the ring to reach him. The mention of sisters alongside mother and brothers, absent from the earlier account of who set out to fetch him, may simply reflect an assumption on the crowd's part rather than a fact — a small, human detail of a message passed along secondhand.
translation: And a crowd was sitting around him, in a circle; and they say to him, Behold, your mother and your brothers, and your sisters, are outside seeking you.

label: Mark 3:33–35
text: The verb behind "looked round about" is built from the same root as the crowd's circle in the previous verse — Jesus's gaze sweeps the whole ring of people seated around him. It's the same kind of encompassing look he gave the Pharisees back in verse 5, but the temperature is entirely different: no anger here, nothing but warmth. And there's a small but telling grammatical signal in what follows — "brother," "sister," and "mother" all appear without the definite article that would normally accompany them in Greek, marking them as figurative rather than literal. Jesus isn't redefining his family in a moment of estrangement; he's naming a family built on obedience to God that anyone in that circle could belong to.
translation: And sweeping his gaze around the whole circle of those seated about him, he says, Behold my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, the same is brother, and sister, and mother, to me.

label: Mark 4:2
text: "He taught" renders an imperfect tense — not a single lecture but continuous action, session after session. Mark reaches for this tense often, and it does the work of a moving picture rather than a snapshot. Two verbs cover the range of Jesus's public speech: didaskō, "to teach," the patient unfolding of a subject point by point, and kērussō, "to proclaim," the herald's public announcement. It's worth noting that the New Testament never once calls Jesus a kērux, a "proclaimer" — the title people reached for was always didaskalos, "teacher." His parables were exactly what didaskō implies: ordinary pictures set alongside a truth to make it graspable, pitched to what his hearers could actually take in.
translation: And he kept on teaching them many things in illustrations laid alongside the truth, session after session, and kept saying to them in his teaching.

label: Mark 4:3
text: "Hearken" translates akouete, a present-tense imperative — "keep on listening" — rather than the clipped, almost military snap available in the Greek aorist imperative for a blunt command. Jesus chose the gentler form. He needed a shoreline crowd to settle in and stay attentive while he spoke from a boat just offshore, and he got there by patience rather than a bark of authority. "Behold" (idou) is a small attention-getting particle with no tidy English equivalent, closer to "look here" than a formal "behold" — inserted simply to give the moment an extra jolt of immediacy.
translation: Keep on listening: Look here, the sower went out to sow.

label: Mark 4:4
text: "Wayside" is simply hodos, "road" — the hard-packed path running alongside or through the field, not part of the cultivated ground at all. Seed landing there never had a chance to work into soil; it sat exposed on the surface until the birds found it.
translation: And it came to pass, as he sowed, that some seed fell along the hard-packed path, and the birds came and devoured it up.

label: Mark 4:5
text: "Some" translates allo, "another seed of the same kind." Mark is careful to note that the seed itself never varies from patch to patch in the story. Whatever different fates befall it, the difference traces back to the ground, not the seed — which is the whole point of the parable: the Word sown doesn't change potency from hearer to hearer, but the soil it lands in does.
translation: And another seed, of that same kind, fell on stony ground, where it did not have much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth.

label: Mark 4:7
text:
Again allo marks "another seed of the same kind," this time landing among thorns already established and growing — no farmer sows deliberately into a thicket of briers. "Choked" translates sympnigō, the simple verb "to choke" with the prefix syn, "tightly, together," added — the compound pictures something squeezed shut, throttled, rather than merely crowded. The same verb elsewhere describes a mob pressing in on someone so tightly it threatens to suffocate him.

The following two verses shift into an imperfect verb and present-tense participles — "kept on yielding," "growing up," "increasing," "kept on bearing" — grammar chosen to stretch a flat fact ("it bore fruit") into a process still unfolding as the story is told.
translation:
And another seed of that same kind fell among the thorns already grown up, and the thorns rose up and throttled it, squeezing it shut, and it kept on yielding no fruit.

And other seeds fell into the good ground, and kept on yielding fruit, growing up and increasing continually, and kept on bearing, some thirty, and some sixty, and some a hundred.

label: Mark 4:10
text:
"They that were about him" names a different circle than "those closest to him" back in chapter 3 — not his skeptical family, but the wider ring of followers from which the Twelve had been drawn. "The mystery" translates mystērion, built on a root meaning "to shut, to close" — the same word the pagan mystery-cults used for truths known only to initiates. Scripture keeps the shape of the word but changes its content: not a truth that's merely hard to work out, but one impossible to grasp until God discloses it — and then perfectly plain.

"Is given" is a perfect tense: not "was handed to you once" but "stands given to you, and remains yours." The disciples had received the secret of the Kingdom as a lasting possession, theirs to grow into rather than something they'd have to re-earn. "That" (hina) introduces a purpose clause, "in order that" — the parables are said to function so as to open the truth to the receptive while, at the same time, sealing the willfully closed-minded deeper into their own blindness. It's the same pattern Scripture shows elsewhere: light refused eventually blinds the one who refused it.
translation: And when he was alone, those about him, along with the twelve, kept asking him about the illustration. And he said to them, To you the secret of the kingdom of God stands given, and remains yours; but to those who are outside, all things come in illustrations laid alongside the truth: in order that seeing they may see and not perceive, and hearing they may hear and not understand.

label: Mark 4:13
text: The question carries a note of surprised reproach — these men have already been let in on the secret of the Kingdom, and the parable still eludes them. The definite article before "parables" points to a specific body of teaching, what Jesus has already given and what is still coming, and the force of the question is that the Sower functions as a kind of master key: miss this one, and the rest stay shut. "How" translates pōs, carrying the sense "how is it even possible" — not a request for information but Jesus registering, out loud, that without this parable none of the others can be understood.
translation: And he says to them, Do you not understand this illustration? How, then, will you understand all the illustrations?

label: Mark 4:15
text:
Two words for "evil" sit behind the New Testament's language for the enemy. Kakos names evil in the abstract — a flaw, a defect, something simply bad. Ponēros (the word Matthew's parallel uses for "the evil one") names evil that is actively aggressive, not content to be corrupt itself but bent on dragging others down too. Luke's parallel calls him ho diabolos, "the slanderer, the false accuser." All three accounts attach the definite article — not "an adversary" but "the adversary," a specific, known figure. "Taketh away" (airō) means to seize by force what belongs to, or has been entrusted to, someone else. And "that was sown" is a perfect participle — a completed act with a lasting result: the Word had already lodged in the heart and begun its work before it was snatched away.

The next few verses supply their own vocabulary for the other soils. "Cares" (merimna) comes from a root meaning "pulled in different directions" — the New Testament's word for anxious distraction, not ordinary concern. "World" here is aiōn, "age," the present course of life lived apart from God, not the physical earth. And "lusts" is a word whose meaning has drifted in English — the Greek simply means "strong desire," good or bad depending on what it's attached to, only later narrowing to something illicit.
translation:
And these are they by the path, where the word is sown: and when they have heard, immediately the adversary comes and seizes by force the word that had been sown, and had already lodged, in their hearts.

And these likewise are they sown among the thorns: such as hear the word, and the anxieties, pulled in different directions, of this present age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the strong desires for other things entering in, throttle the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

label: Mark 4:21
text: The question opens with mēti, a negative particle that expects the answer "no" — "a lamp doesn't come..., does it?" Mark personifies the object with erchetai, "come," as though the lamp walked into the room on its own — part of his habitually vivid way of telling a story. "Bushel" is modios, a dry-measure container about the size of a peck basket; clamping a lit lamp under one would smother the flame outright. "Bed" is klinē, the low reclining couch set beside a dining table — households of the day ate lying down, not seated — and shoving a lamp under one would set the furniture on fire rather than hide the light. The two images fail in opposite directions to make one point: conceal a lamp and you either extinguish it or destroy something. Its place is the stand (lychnia), out where it can do the one thing it exists to do.
translation: And he kept saying to them, A lamp doesn't come in to be put under the peck-measure, or under the couch, does it? Doesn't it come in to be set upon the lampstand?

label: Mark 4:22
text: The verse is often misread as promising that every secret will eventually leak out. The actual claim runs the other direction: things are hidden for a time precisely so that they can later be revealed — concealment as the means to disclosure, not its opposite. "Manifested" translates phaneroō, "to make visible or known what was previously hidden or unknown." The parables' obscurity has a built-in expiration date; what the disciples hold privately now, they'll be responsible to proclaim openly once the time comes.
translation: For there is nothing hidden, except that it should be made visible; nor was anything kept secret, except that it should come into the open.

label: Mark 4:23
text:
The condition here uses ei, the particle for a condition assumed to be true, rather than ean, which would mark something merely hypothetical. The premise isn't in question — the hearers genuinely do have ears. What's in question is whether they'll use them, and both the infinitive and the main verb are present tense, stressing sustained attentiveness rather than a single act of hearing: "let him keep on hearing."

The verb behind "shall more be given" (prostithēmi) carries the prefix pros, "toward" — the sense is of something added on top of what's already due, out of proportion to the effort spent earning it. The measure of attention a person brings to what they hear becomes, almost mechanically, the measure of what comes back to them.

The parable that follows shifts tenses deliberately. "Should cast seed" is an aorist subjunctive, naming the bare act of sowing without dwelling on details. "Should sleep and rise" and "should spring and grow" are present tense, picturing repeated, ordinary days passing while growth happens unseen — the Greek word order even puts special weight on "how": the farmer doesn't know how the seed grows, only that it does.

A final detail is worth keeping: "of herself" (automatē, the word behind our "automatic") describes something self-moved, proceeding under its own power rather than external control — used elsewhere in the New Testament only of a gate swinging open on its own. The stages of growth get their own precise vocabulary too — chortos, the first blade of grass out of the ground; stachys, the forming ear; sitos, the ripened grain itself — a small botanical ladder tracking a process no farmer can rush and no farmer fully controls.
translation:
If any man genuinely has ears to hear, let him keep on hearing.

Take heed what you hear: with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you; and to you who hear shall more be added, over and above, out of proportion to what you brought.

And he kept saying, So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed upon the earth, and should sleep and rise, night and day, and the seed keeps springing up and growing, he knows not how. The earth of herself, moved by her own power, bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

label: Mark 4:30
text:
"Liken" translates homoioō, "to compare, to find a resemblance between two things." The first-person plural, "shall we liken," draws the hearers themselves into the search for the right picture rather than simply handing them an answer.

The mustard seed that follows plays on real, verifiable smallness at planting and real, visible size at maturity — the definite article on "herbs" specifies cultivated garden plants, not wild ones, sharpening the contrast between the tiniest seed a gardener would plant and the biggest plant that garden would produce. "Lodge" is literally "pitch their tents," the same picture language used of nomads camping.

The closing note on Jesus's method turns on a double sense of akouō, "to hear": in certain New Testament contexts (as elsewhere in the epistles) the word slides from mere hearing into understanding, and that's the sense at work here — Jesus pitched his teaching to what his audience could actually take in, not just what they could physically hear. "Spake he not" is imperfect, marking habitual practice, not a one-time exception. And "he expounded" is epiluō — the simple verb "to loosen" with the perfective prefix epi added, "to loosen further," i.e., to unpack and clarify well past the surface meaning. In private, with the Twelve — idios marking them as peculiarly his own circle, not the wider crowd of learners — that loosening amounted to something closer to fresh disclosure than mere explanation.
translation:
And he kept saying, To what shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is smaller than all the seeds that are upon the earth; but when it is sown, it grows up, and becomes greater than all the garden herbs, and puts out great branches, so that the birds of the air are able to pitch their tents under its shadow.

And with many such illustrations laid alongside the truth he kept speaking the word to them, as they were able to hear and understand it; and without an illustration he did not habitually speak to them: but privately, to his own, he loosened everything further, unpacking it all.

label: Mark 4:35
text: Mark rarely bothers to anchor an episode to a specific time of day, which makes his notice here — "the same day," evening having come — worth pausing on. It ties the crossing of the lake directly onto the end of the long day of parables, the accusation, and the visit from his family: the storm on the water follows hard on a day that had already drained him.
translation: And on that same day, when evening had come, he says to them, Let us go across to the other side.

label: Mark 4:36
text: "They took him" renders paralambanō — the simple verb "to take" with the prefix "alongside" attached, giving the sense of taking someone under one's care and protection.
