The same verb describes the angel telling Joseph to take the child and his mother to Egypt: not a casual pickup, but a deliberate assuming of responsibility. "Ship" is ploion, the larger fishing vessel, not a rowboat — the traditional "little ships" for the accompanying boats rests on a weaker manuscript reading; the better texts have the same, larger word both times.
translation: And leaving the crowd, they took him under their care, along with them, in the boat, the larger vessel, even as he was. And other boats also were with him.

label: Mark 4:37
text: The word behind "there arose a great storm" never describes a single strong gust or even a steadily blowing wind, however violent — it names a storm that breaks suddenly out of black thunderclouds, a whirlwind driving rain and chaos in every direction at once, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the whirlwind out of which God spoke to Job. "Beat into" (epiballō, "to throw upon") is imperfect tense — the waves weren't crashing in once but repeatedly, wave after wave. "Was now full" uses gemizō, "to fill up" — the boat was in the process of swamping as the disciples watched.
translation: And there arises a great whirlwind of a storm, out of the black clouds, and the waves kept beating into the boat, over and over, so that the boat was now, even as they watched, filling up with water.

label: Mark 4:38
text: "The hinder part" is prymna, the stern, the opposite end from the bow. "Pillow" (proskephalaion, literally "that toward which one puts the head") was no soft luxury cushion but the steersman's leather headrest or the low bench where he sat — ordinary ship's furniture, not comfort brought along for the trip. "Master" in the disciples' cry is didaskale, the vocative of "Teacher," the same title Mark has already shown was the one people instinctively reached for. "Carest thou not" uses a verb (mellei) meaning "it is a concern, a care" — and "we perish" is present tense, "we are perishing" right now, not a prediction of what's about to happen. The disciples aren't warning him of coming danger; they're reporting an emergency already underway that he's sleeping through.
translation: And he himself was in the stern, asleep on the steersman's headrest: and they wake him, and say to him, Teacher, is it no concern to you that we are perishing, right now?

label: Mark 4:39
text: "Peace" translates siōpaō, "be silent, hushed, calm," in the present imperative — "be being calmed," an ongoing settling rather than an instant. "Be still" is phimoō, "to muzzle" — literally the verb for putting a muzzle on an ox, used elsewhere of Jesus silencing hostile questioners. Here it's a perfect imperative: "be muzzled, and stay that way." The command to the wind is for a process of quieting; the command to the sea is for an immediate and permanent hush. "Ceased" (kopazō) pictures the wind as if it had worn itself out, grown tired of raging — vivid personification matching the storm's own violent introduction two verses earlier.
translation: And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, Be silent, be continually calmed; be muzzled, and stay muzzled. And the wind grew weary and ceased, and there was a great calm.

label: Mark 4:40
text: "Fearful" is an adjective doing the work of a noun — "you timid ones, you fearful ones." "How is it" translates pōs, the same construction used back in verse 13 for "how is it possible" — Jesus isn't asking a real question so much as expressing astonishment that men who have watched him this closely could still lack faith. The one who had just quieted a hurricane with two sentences was sitting in the boat with them the whole time.
translation: And he said to them, Why are you so timid? How is it that you still have no faith?

label: Mark 4:41
text: "They feared exceedingly" is literally "they feared a great fear" — a noun repeating and intensifying its own verb, a Hebraic idiom carried straight into the Greek for maximum force. "What manner of man" oversets the original: the word "man" isn't in the Greek at all, and Mark's actual wording is simply "who then is this?" — with ara, "then," functioning as an inferential particle: given everything that's just happened, who must this be? The demonstrative is masculine, so a person, not a force or a phenomenon, is what's being asked about. Wind and sea taking orders from a human voice is what turns the disciples' fear of the storm into something closer to awe of the man in the boat with them.
translation: And they feared a great fear, and kept saying to one another, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

label: Mark 5:2–5
text:
The man's dwelling place uses a compound verb built on the preposition kata, "down" — the same idea behind our phrase "settled down." Combined with the imperfect tense of "had," the picture is of a man who had made the tombs his permanent, ongoing residence, not a temporary hideout. The tombs themselves were often natural caves or chambers cut into the rock, roomy enough to be held up by pillars, with recesses along the walls for the dead — set apart from the towns, in lonely country, exactly the kind of place a man fleeing all human company would gravitate to.

"Chain" translates halusis, itself built from luo, "to loose," with a negating prefix — literally "that which cannot be loosed." Paul uses the same word of the handcuffs he wore as a prisoner (Ephesians 6:20) and of Onesiphorus's chain (2 Timothy 1:16). Here the irony is that this chain kept failing at its own name: "bound with fetters and chains" uses a perfect-tense verb describing careful, thorough work, yet "plucked asunder" (diaspao, "torn in two") and "broken in pieces" (suntribo, "crushed together") describe the man's superhuman strength snapping every restraint, so that no one had the power to "tame" him — damazo, the word for breaking a wild animal. His cry (krazo) was an inarticulate shriek, and his self-mutilation (katakopto, "to cut oneself up") left him gashed and scarred from head to foot.
translation: And there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, who had continually made his dwelling among the tombs; and no one was able to bind him any longer, not even with a chain, because he had often been bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him and the fetters crushed to pieces, and no one had the strength to tame him. And always, night and day, he was in the tombs and in the mountains, crying out and cutting himself with stones.

label: Mark 5:6–8
text:
The word rendered "but" is simply kai, plain "and" — Greek has two stronger words for "but" (alla and de) that Mark doesn't reach for here. The connection is continuative, not contrastive: this violent man's usual behavior toward strangers and his sudden run toward Jesus are simply two things that happened in sequence, not a dramatic reversal the grammar itself signals. What happens next is the reversal — proskuneo, "worship," describes falling to the knees and touching the forehead to the ground, the full posture of homage paid to a king or to God. A being given over to darkness, with no salvation offered him, bows to the Son of God here just as Paul says every being under the earth will (Philippians 2:10) — though it is the demon controlling the man, not the man himself, who renders this forced homage.

"What have I to do with thee" is more literally "what is there with reference to me and with reference to you" — an idiom asking, "what do we have in common?" The demon then puts Jesus under an oath: "I adjure thee" translates horkizo, "to force someone to swear." "Torment" is basanizo, a word that originally described testing metal on a touchstone before it came to mean torture — the demon's version of the third degree, in reverse. And "for He said" is a progressive imperfect, "He had been saying" — Jesus had already commanded the spirit out more than once; this outburst is the demon's response to a command already repeated.
translation: And seeing Jesus from afar, he ran and worshiped him, and crying out with a loud voice he said, What is there between me and you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I put you under oath by God, do not torment me. For Jesus had been saying to him, Come out of the man, you unclean spirit.

label: Mark 5:9
text: "He asked him" is imperfect — "he kept on asking" — implying the demon didn't answer on the first try. "Legion" was a fixed, well-known term for a Roman military unit of roughly 6,800 men, already borrowed into both Greek and Aramaic in this region where legions were a familiar sight. The name isn't picked for size alone but for what a legion represented: overwhelming, organized force. One man, but many spirits operating as a single unit under that name.
translation: And he kept on asking him, What is your name? And he answered, saying, Legion is my name, for we are many.

label: Mark 5:10
text:
"Besought Him much" is imperfect of parakaleo, "I beg you, please" — the demon kept pleading, speaking for the whole company inhabiting the man, that they not be sent out of the region altogether. "Decapolis" is simply the transliteration of the Greek for "ten cities," the district just southeast of the Sea of Galilee.

When the request narrows to the herd of swine, the verb shifts to the aorist — a single decisive plea rather than ongoing pressure — and "send" is an aorist imperative, a sharp command wanting instant compliance. The demons' request itself is telling: it implies they have no rest apart from occupying a body, human or animal, which is why exile from every possible host was the one thing worse to them than entering swine.
translation: And he kept begging him urgently that he would not send them out of the region.

label: Mark 5:13
text:
Jesus doesn't command the demons into the swine — He permits it; the grammar keeps the initiative with them, not with Him. "Ran violently" is hormao, "to rush headlong, to be driven forward with sudden force" — the same shock of unwelcome occupation that had made the man himself unmanageable now sent two thousand animals stampeding down the slope. "Were choked" is imperfect, picturing the herd disappearing into the water pig by pig rather than all at once; the verb is also used elsewhere of drowning.

The swineherds "fled" (pheugo, to run for safety) and gave a full, detailed report (diegeomai, "to narrate all the way through") to their employers — understandably eager to explain a wrecked herd. When the townspeople came to look, "see" translates theoreo, the word for a searching, deliberate inspection rather than a passing glance — the kind of scrutiny a general gives troops on review. What they found undid them more than the loss of the pigs: the former demoniac "in his right mind," sophroneo, a word whose dominant sense is self-control, a settled rein on one's own passions and desires, not bare sanity. A man who used to gash himself with stones was now sitting still, dressed, and master of himself — and it was that transformation, even more than the wrecked herd, that sent the town begging Jesus to leave.
translation: And he permitted them. And the unclean spirits came out and entered into the swine, and the herd, about two thousand, rushed headlong down the steep bank into the sea, and one by one they were being choked in the sea. And those who fed them fled and reported the whole matter fully, both in the town and in the country. And they came to inspect closely what had happened, and came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in full possession of himself, the very man who had had the legion; and they were afraid.

label: Mark 5:18
text: The verb describing Jesus stepping into the boat is a present participle running alongside the main verb "prayed" — the man's pleading happened in the very moment of Jesus boarding, as if he couldn't risk missing the chance. His request to go along looks like a bid to become a disciple, though it's just as easily read as simple fear of being left alone again in the place where the spirits had found him.
translation: And as he was stepping into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed kept begging him that he might be with him.

label: Mark 5:19
text:
"Go home to thy friends" is more exactly "go into your home, to your own" — Jesus sends him first to his own family, the people who had presumably watched his years of torment. "Tell" is apaggello, "to carry a report back" — bring them word of what happened. "Hath done" is perfect tense, marking a complete, settled result: this was not a temporary improvement but a finished cure. "Had compassion" translates eleeo, sympathy for another's suffering specifically of the kind that acts, not merely feels.

Elsewhere Jesus silences those He heals, wary of stirring the wrong kind of excitement about His mission. Here there's no such danger — the townspeople had just begged Him to leave — and this district needed the testimony badly enough that Jesus sends the man out to give it.
translation: Go into your home, to your own people, and report back to them how much the Lord has done for you, and stands done, and how he had mercy on you.

label: Mark 5:20
text: "Publish" is kerusso, "to make a public proclamation," the word for a herald's announcement, not a private conversation. "Decapolis" again is just "ten cities" transliterated — and the man took his testimony across the whole district, so that this healed man became known, by report, throughout all ten towns.
translation: And he went away and began to proclaim publicly in the Ten Cities how much Jesus had done for him; and everyone was marveling.

label: Mark 5:21
text:
"Gathered unto Him" is literally "after Him" (epi), not simply "to Him" — the crowd forms behind Him as He becomes the center everyone orients toward. The verb "was gathered" is passive: the people didn't organize themselves so much as get pulled together by a force outside themselves, drawn by the pull of who He was. "Nigh unto the sea" uses para, "alongside" — He is right at the water's edge.

A synagogue normally had more than one ruler (compare Acts 13:14-15), whose duties included choosing readers and teachers and keeping order in services — so Jairus held real local standing. His name is Hebrew for "whom the Lord enlightens." "At the point of death" is an idiom, literally "she has it lastly" — she is breathing her last. And the word Jairus uses isn't the ordinary word for "heal" but sozo, "save" — the same word used of spiritual salvation, here carrying its equally legitimate sense of rescue from death, exactly as we still say a dying patient's life was "saved."
translation: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd was gathered together after him, and he was alongside the sea. And there comes one of the synagogue rulers, Jairus by name, and seeing him, falls at his feet, and begs him earnestly, saying, My little daughter is at her last gasp; come and lay your hands on her, that she may be saved and live.

label: Mark 5:24
text:
"Jesus went with him" more fully reads "went off with him at once" — no hesitation. "Much people followed" is imperfect, a crowd that kept pressing along behind Him the whole way, and "thronged" (sunthlibo) means pressed in from every side — Luke's parallel account uses a word for crowding someone to the point of suffocation.

"Suffered" (25-26) is pascho, "to suffer pain," not merely "to undergo treatment" — this woman's twelve years were years of real pain, spent "under" (hupo) the hands of many doctors who left her worse, not better.

When she "heard of Jesus" (27-28), the Greek has a definite article that the English drops: she heard about "the Jesus" — a small detail that shows how common the name Joshua/Jesus was, and how the article had become a way of marking out this particular Jesus, whose reputation by now needed no further introduction. Coming up in the crowd behind Him, she kept saying to herself — the verb is imperfect — "if I touch even His garments, I shall be sozo," the same word Jairus used: saved, whether from disease or from anything else, one word for both.
translation: And he went off with him at once. And a great crowd kept following him, and kept pressing in on him from every side.

label: Mark 5:29
text: "The fountain of her blood was dried up" uses pege, "spring" — not just that the flow stopped, but that its source was shut off, a picture chosen to say the cure was total, not temporary relief. "She felt" translates ginosko, "to know by personal experience," and the tense is the ingressive aorist — the instant of realization, the moment it dawned on her that something had changed. "She was healed of that plague" is perfect tense, "I have been healed and remain so." "Plague" is mastix, literally "whip" or "scourge" — the same word used elsewhere of suffering regarded as discipline from God's hand. Twelve years of being scourged by this illness, ended in an instant.
translation: And immediately the spring of her blood was dried up at its source, and she came to know in her body that she had been healed, and remained healed, of her scourge.

label: Mark 5:30
text: "Knowing" is epiginosko — the simple verb already means experiential, personal knowledge, and the prefix epi sharpens it further, giving the sense of a clear, unmistakable awareness. What He knew was that dunamis — "power," specifically the kind that overcomes resistance and produces change — had gone out from Him. The Greek word order itself puts the emphasis where it belongs: "the out-from-Him power going out." Some measure of what made the miracle happen cost Him something to give; He felt it leave.
translation: And Jesus, immediately becoming clearly and unmistakably aware within himself that power had gone out from him, turned about in the crowd and kept saying, Who touched my garments?

label: Mark 5:31
text: The word for "thronging" here (sunthlibo) is a compound of thlibo, the verb Mark uses back in 3:9 for ordinary crowd-pressure — but thlibo is also the word for pressing grapes at the winepress, crushing them. Adding the prefix sun, "together," intensifies it further: a concerted, converging press from every direction, worse than usual. The disciples' surprise is genuine — in a crush like that, why single out one touch? — but their question misses that Jesus was registering something the crowd's random jostling could never produce.
translation: And his disciples kept saying to him, You see the crowd pressing in on you together from every side, crushing in on you, and yet you say, Who touched me?

label: Mark 5:32
text: "He looked round about" is imperfect and middle voice together — continuous action, done for His own purpose, in His own interest — Jesus keeps searching the crowd on His own initiative regardless of what the disciples had just objected. The Greek article and participle describing "her who had done this" are feminine, marking out a woman specifically. Whatever told Him that, the distinction was real: her touch, however brief, was categorically different from the crowd's shoving — timid, deliberate, and, given what Levitical law said about her condition, genuinely risky for her to attempt at all.
translation: And he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.

label: Mark 5:33
text: "What was done" is perfect tense — a completed, lasting change, which is exactly why she couldn't simply melt back into the crowd once she realized she'd been seen. She had touched Him in secret, aware that what she'd done broke ceremonial boundaries, and now falls before Him and discloses "all the truth" — not just the touch itself but the whole account behind it, years of illness and every reason she had for reaching out the way she did.
translation: But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done in her and stood done, came and fell down before him and told him all the truth.

label: Mark 5:34
text: "Daughter" is the first word out of His mouth to her, and it's deliberately chosen — not a term for a child but a term of tenderness, spoken to a grown woman probably close to His own age. It reframes the entire encounter: not power dispensed to a stranger, but a father's welcome to his own. "Hath made thee whole" is sozo again, perfect tense — a permanent rescue, sealed. "Go in peace" uses the preposition eis, "into," not "in" — not simply accompanied by peace but sent forward into it, as through a door just opened for her. "Be whole" is a present imperative, "keep on being whole" — hugies, "sound of body," the root behind our word "hygienic" — of her mastix, that same "scourge" word from a few verses earlier, now closed for good.
translation: And he said to her, Daughter, your faith has saved you, and the salvation stands. Go your way into peace, and continue being sound and whole from your scourge.

label: Mark 5:35
text: "There came" is a historical present — Mark's Greek switches to present tense mid-narrative for vividness, dropping the reader into the moment as it happened. "Thy daughter is dead" is aorist: a flat, completed fact — "she died." The word "house" isn't actually in the Greek; it's supplied because the ruler himself is standing right there with Jesus, so the messengers must be coming from his home. "Troublest" is skullo, a vivid word literally meaning "to skin" or "flay" before it came to mean "bother, harass, wear out" — the messengers assume the case is now closed and see no point in dragging out the Teacher's (didaskalos) time any further.
translation: While he was yet speaking, there come some from the ruler's house who say, Your daughter died. Why do you go on wearing out the Teacher?

label: Mark 5:36
text: "Jesus heard" is parakouo, "to hear alongside" — to overhear something not addressed to Him. "Be not afraid" is a present imperative used as a prohibition, and this construction specifically forbids continuing an action already underway: not "don't start being afraid" but "stop the fear you're already in." "Only believe" is also a present imperative, and it carries the same continuous force in the other direction — "keep on believing," a sustained, ongoing trust Jesus calls for precisely at the moment the news seems to have closed off all reason for it.
translation: But Jesus, overhearing the word being spoken, says to the ruler of the synagogue, Stop being afraid; only keep on believing.

label: Mark 5:37
text: The Greek attaches the definite article to Peter's name alone, which has the effect of binding all three men — Peter, James, and John — together as a single, recognized unit, set apart from the rest. These three alone are allowed to witness what follows; the training of the Twelve had its inner circle, and this was one of the moments reserved for it.
translation: And he permitted no one to accompany him except Peter, and James, and John the brother of James.

label: Mark 5:38
text: The best manuscripts read "they come," not "He cometh" — Jesus, the ruler, and the three disciples arrive together. "Seeth" is theoreo, the same word for a deliberate, searching look used earlier of the crowd examining the healed demoniac — Jesus takes in the scene with full understanding, not surprise. "Tumult" is thorubos, "uproar," and "wailed" (alalazo) is an onomatopoeic word — its very sound imitates the cry it names, the same shout soldiers once raised charging into battle, here worn down into the professional, repetitive keening of hired mourners.
translation: And they come to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and he looks closely and takes in an uproar, and people weeping and wailing loudly, again and again.

label: Mark 5:39
text: "Why make ye this ado" uses thorubeo, "to raise an uproar" — the same root as the "tumult" just described. "Damsel" is paidion, "little girl." "Is dead" is aorist — a plain statement of the fact, not a denial of it. When Jesus calls it "sleep," He isn't disputing that she died; He's naming what death is about to become in His hands — a condition He is about to reverse as easily as waking someone.
translation: And going in, he says to them, Why do you raise this uproar, and weep? The little girl did not die, but is sleeping.

label: Mark 5:40
text: "Laughed Him to scorn" is katagelao — the ordinary verb "to laugh" with a prefix meaning "down," so literally "to laugh someone down," to jeer. The tense is inceptive imperfect: "they broke out laughing and kept at it." "Put them all out" is ekballo, "to throw out" — real physical force was apparently needed to clear the professional mourners from the house, much as it had been needed to clear the Temple. "Taketh" is paralambano, "to take alongside," of gathering the parents and the three disciples under His own direct charge. And "entereth" uses eisporeuomai, a verb elsewhere used of setting out on a journey, rather than one of the plainer words for simply walking — as if the few steps into that room carried the weight of a much longer road, the way a short walk can feel endless when everything about the destination matters.
translation: And they began laughing him down, and kept at it. But he, throwing them all out, takes along with him the father of the little girl and the mother and those with him, and sets out into where the little girl was lying.

label: Mark 5:41
text: He took the girl's hand with krateo, "to grip firmly, to take possession of" — a strong, deliberate hold, the kind needed to help someone weakened by illness rise. "Talitha cumi" preserves Jesus's actual Aramaic words, remembered and passed on — almost certainly through Peter, who was in the room — then translated into Greek for readers who didn't speak the original. The same pattern shows up with Jesus's words from the cross: the original language kept, then rendered for a wider audience. A tender, private moment gets its native words preserved rather than smoothed into translation alone.
translation: And gripping the little girl's hand firmly, he says to her, Talitha cumi, which is, being translated, Little girl, I say to you, arise.

label: Mark 5:42
text: "Arose" is anistemi, "to stand up," aorist tense — a single completed action, someone getting up from lying down. "Walked" shifts to the imperfect of peripateo, "kept on walking about" — not one step but sustained, ordinary movement. The note that she "was twelve years" old matters because paidion, "little girl," could otherwise suggest a much younger child; the detail confirms she was old enough to be up and walking under her own power. "Astonished with a great astonishment" uses existemi, literally "to stand out of" or "to be put out of place" — the source of our word "ecstasy," though "amazement," people knocked clean out of their ordinary composure, captures the sense better than anything mystical.
translation: And immediately the little girl stood up, and kept walking about; for she was twelve years old. And at once they were utterly beside themselves with a great amazement.

label: Mark 5:43
text: "Charged them straitly" is diastello, "to give strict orders." The concern wasn't that people would notice the girl was alive and well — that couldn't be hidden — but that word of an actual return from death would spread and stir up the wrong kind of expectation. The instruction to give her something to eat is a small, practical detail: not merely alive, but well enough to need supper, proof that this was a full restoration and not a fragile reprieve.
translation: And he gave them strict orders that no one should know this, and he told them to give her something to eat.

label: Mark 6:2
text: "Astonished" translates ekplēssō, built from a prefix meaning "out" attached to the verb "to strike" — the picture is of being struck clean out of one's composure, stunned past self-possession rather than merely startled. The verb is imperfect: this was not a moment's gasp but a lingering daze that hung over the synagogue crowd. Their own neighbor, a man they had watched grow up in a carpenter's shop, was suddenly displaying wisdom and dunamis — the New Testament's word for miracle-working power breaking in from outside the natural order — that nothing about His hometown pedigree could account for. Their question, "from where does this one get these things?" is clipped and biting in the Greek, less a genuine inquiry than a demand that He justify Himself.
translation: And many, hearing him, kept on being astonished, struck out of their composure, saying, From where does this man get these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him, that even such works of power come about through his hands?

label: Mark 6:3
text: "Carpenter" renders tektōn, a word broader than the English suggests — it covered anyone who built or shaped material for a living, in wood, stone, or metal, essentially a skilled tradesman. Jesus had earned His bread with His hands for roughly three decades before anyone heard Him teach. That gap — common laborer one year, extraordinary teacher and healer the next — is exactly what tripped up His neighbors. "Offended" translates skandalizō, the word for the trigger of a trap: something that causes a person to stumble over what should have led them to trust. They could not reconcile the carpenter they knew with the authority they were hearing, so instead of bridging the gap with faith, they let it become the very thing that tripped them.
translation: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James, and Joses, and Judas, and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? And they kept being tripped up over him, stumbling on him as on a trap.

label: Mark 6:4
text: "Prophet" is prophētēs, literally one who speaks forth — a herald of God's message, not primarily a predictor of the future, which is a secondary sense English has layered onto the word. Using it of Himself here, Jesus claims a specific office alongside the other titles He had already claimed elsewhere — Messiah, Son of Man, Son of God. "Honor" is timē, the recognition and deference a person is owed. The irony Jesus names is almost proverbial: distance breeds reverence, familiarity breeds contempt. The people with the most exposure to Him — His own household, His own town — extended Him the least of it.
translation: And Jesus kept saying to them, A prophet is not without honor, except in his own fatherland, and among his own relatives, and in his own house.

label: Mark 6:5
text: The negation is emphatic in the Greek — not simply "no" mighty work, but "not even one." "Sick" translates arrōstos, a word for weakness at the constitutional level, a body without strength, rather than any specific ailment. "Work" again is dunamis, the vocabulary of supernatural power breaking into ordinary life. The picture is not that Jesus's power failed Him in Nazareth; it's that unbelief had closed off the channel through which it normally flowed — so thoroughly that the townspeople didn't even trouble themselves to bring their sick to Him.
translation: And he was not able to do there not even one work of power, except that he laid his hands on a few who were without strength, and healed them.

label: Mark 6:6
text: Jesus "marvelled" at their unbelief — the same capacity for astonishment the Gospels elsewhere show Him exercising toward a Gentile centurion's faith, here provoked by its opposite. That a teacher who knows all things could still marvel is worth sitting with: as God, nothing catches Him by surprise, yet in His genuine humanity He came to Nazareth carrying an expectation, and what He met there disappointed it. "He went about the villages" pictures a circuit — Jesus working the ring of towns surrounding Nazareth, teaching His way around the very region that had just shut Him out.
translation: And he kept marveling because of their unbelief. And he went around the villages in a circuit, teaching.

label: Mark 6:7
text:
"He calls to Himself the Twelve" — Mark's Greek is present tense even though narrating a past event, his habit of throwing a scene into the present to make it vivid. The verb for sending them out is apostellō, the root of our word "apostle": not a casual dispatch but a formal commissioning, envoys sent to represent the Sender's own authority. What they carry is exousia — delegated authority — over the unclean spirits, distinct from dunamis, the raw power itself; the Twelve are given the right to command, backed by a power that isn't their own.

The travel restrictions are pointed. No pēra — not merely "no travel bag" but no beggar's collecting-pouch, the kind itinerant religious hucksters carried to gather offerings from onlookers; Jesus is ruling out professional begging, not just packing light. No chalkos, "copper" — no money at all, in the coinage a poor traveler would actually carry. And shaking the dust off their feet when a topos, a town or district, refused to receive them, was a recognized gesture of formal repudiation — a visible verdict pronounced on a place that had heard and refused.

Their message, that people should repent, uses metanoeō — literally a change of mind about one's former course, not an emotion of regret (the New Testament keeps a separate word for that). And "anointed with oil" reflects the ordinary medicinal use of olive oil in the ancient world, the era's basic remedy, used here alongside the disciples' healing ministry — prayer and means working together, not one replacing the other.
translation: And he calls to himself the Twelve, and began to send them out two by two, and kept giving them authority over the unclean spirits; and he charged them that they should take nothing for the road except a staff only — no bread, no beggar's pouch, no copper coin in their belts; and that they should change their minds. And they kept casting out many demons, and kept anointing with oil many who were without strength, and kept healing them.

label: Mark 6:14
text: Matthew and Luke both call Herod "tetrarch," his technical title as one of four regional rulers; Mark, writing for a Roman audience where the term was applied loosely to any eastern potentate, calls him "king" — not an error, just a difference in audience. "Shew forth" translates energeō, the verb for energy actively at work; "mighty works" is again dunamis. Herod's theory — that John, raised from the dead, was now channeling a supernatural power he never displayed in life — reads less like careful theology and more like the guesswork of a guilty conscience straining to explain something it can't simply dismiss.
translation: And King Herod heard of it, for his name had become well known; and he kept saying, John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead, and because of this these powers are actively at work in him.

label: Mark 6:15
text: The other theories in circulation — that Jesus was Elijah, or a prophet cut from the same cloth as the old prophets — show people groping for a category large enough to hold what they were seeing. Every explanation reached backward, into the past, because nothing in anyone's present experience offered a live comparison. Nobody guessed the truth: they were out of categories, not out of ideas.
translation: But others kept saying, It is Elijah. And others kept saying, A prophet, like one of the prophets of old.

label: Mark 6:16
text: Herod's verdict lands with the emphasis Greek word order reserves for the front of a sentence: "the one whom I beheaded" comes first, ahead of John's own name — the detail Herod cannot get past. The pronoun "I" is stated outright rather than left buried in the verb ending, and the demonstrative "this one" adds further weight: Herod isn't hedging, he's certain. "Said" is imperfect — he kept repeating the same conclusion every time a fresh theory was floated past him, a man talking himself back into a verdict his conscience had already reached on its own. Mark underscores that it was Herod himself, no proxy, who had ordered John bound — the definite article and an intensive pronoun both drive the point home — because John had told him plainly that his marriage to his brother's wife broke the law.
translation: But Herod, hearing of it, kept repeating, John, whom I myself beheaded — this one has been raised.

label: Mark 6:19
text: "Had a quarrel against him" translates enechō, a verb for settled, simmering hostility — not a passing irritation but a grudge nursed and kept alive. The tense is imperfect: Herodias's anger toward John never let up; she was simply waiting for her opening. "She would have killed him, but she could not" states the situation exactly as it stood — the desire was fully present, only the opportunity was missing.
translation: And Herodias kept a grudge against him and kept wanting to kill him, but she was not able.

label: Mark 6:20
text: "Observed" undersells the verb, suntēreō, which means to actively guard and preserve — Herod was keeping John safe, standing between him and Herodias's designs, not merely watching him with curiosity. The imperfect tense shows this protection held steady over time. The line usually read "he did many things" rests on a textual mix-up; the better reading gives a verb meaning to be at a loss, without resources, unable to find a way through — Herod, torn between a guilty conscience and John's uncompromising preaching, was left perplexed rather than decisive. And "heard him gladly" is likewise imperfect: repeated visits to the prison, a man drawn back again and again to a message that unsettled him every single time.
translation: For Herod kept fearing John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and he kept guarding him safe. And when he heard him, he was thrown into great perplexity; and he kept hearing him gladly.

label: Mark 6:21
text: "Convenient" translates eukairos — built from kairos, a critical, decisive point in time, plus "good": a strategically opportune moment, not simply a free afternoon. Herodias had been waiting for exactly this kind of occasion. The birthday banquet gathered Herod's leading men, his military commanders over units of a thousand, and the chief men of Galilee — a room full of witnesses whose presence would make backing out of a rash promise socially ruinous for Herod, which is precisely the leverage Herodias intended to use.
translation: And a strategically opportune day having come, when Herod on his birthday made a supper for his great men, and the commanders of his thousands, and the chief men of Galilee.

label: Mark 6:22
text: The Greek marks out "the daughter of Herodias" with special emphasis — not just any girl, but Herodias's own daughter, performing a dance of a kind normally reserved for professional entertainers of disreputable standing. That a princess would degrade herself this way before the assembled court was itself part of how the trap worked. Herod's reply — "ask of me whatever you want" — uses thelō, desire rooted in feeling rather than sober judgment: a man carried away by the moment, making a rash promise before he has weighed what it might cost him.
translation: And the daughter of Herodias herself came in and danced, and pleased Herod and those reclining with him. And the king said to the young girl, Ask of me whatever you desire, and I will give it to you.

label: Mark 6:23
text: "He sware" translates omnuō, the verb for formally placing oneself under oath — Herod doesn't just make a promise here, he binds himself to it publicly, raising the stakes of whatever comes next.
translation: And he swore to her, binding himself with an oath, Whatever you ask me, I will give it to you, up to half of my kingdom.

label: Mark 6:24
text: "What shall I ask?" uses a middle-voice construction that marks the girl as acting in her own interest — she goes to consult her mother expecting some prize of her own choosing for herself. What she gets instead is her mother's long-nursed request, handed straight back to her to carry out.
translation: And she went out and said to her mother, What shall I ask for myself? And she said, The head of John the Baptizer.

label: Mark 6:25
text: "With haste" and "straightway" both press the same point: she wastes no time returning to the king, before the mood of the evening could shift or Herod could reconsider. Exautēs, rendered "by and by" in older English, actually means "this instant" — she wants her request granted on the spot, not deferred. The demand itself is phrased with a bluntness that manages to sound even more merciless than the mother who sent her — John's head, at once, on a platter — details calculated to leave Herod no room to soften what he had promised.
translation: And coming in at once with haste to the king, she asked, saying, I want you to give me this instant, on a platter, the head of John the Baptizer.

label: Mark 6:26
text: "Exceedingly sorry" is built from a participle marking entrance into a new state — not "was sorrowful" as an ongoing condition, but "having become sorrowful" at that instant, the moment the request landed. Herod is genuinely shaken. But what decides the outcome isn't his conscience — it's his oath and the roomful of guests who heard him make it. He would rather kill a man he feared and respected than lose face in front of his own court.
translation: And the king, having become deeply grieved, yet because of his oaths and those reclining with him, was not willing to refuse her.

label: Mark 6:27–29
text: "Executioner" is spekoulatōr, a Latin military term imported wholesale into Greek — the word behind our "speculator." It named a member of an imperial bodyguard, the kind of armed escort Roman emperors kept close, and by extension came to carry the sense of a hired killer. Herod's household apes the trappings of Roman court life right down to keeping his own company of these guardsmen on hand — one of whom he now sends, without ceremony, to carry out an execution inside the very prison where John had been kept safe until that day.
translation: And immediately the king, sending out a soldier of his bodyguard, commanded his head to be brought. And going, he beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the young girl; and the young girl gave it to her mother.

label: Mark 6:30
text: "Apostles" here is not yet the fixed, technical title it would later become — it simply describes men sent out on a commission to represent the one who sent them, now returning to report on it. They gather back around Jesus and give their account of everything they had done and taught on the road.
translation: And the sent-out ones gather themselves together to Jesus, and reported to him all things, both what they had done and what they had taught.

label: Mark 6:31
text: "Come ye yourselves apart" piles up an emphasis in the Greek that flattens out in English translation — the pronoun for "you" doesn't need to be there grammatically at all, since the verb ending already carries the person, so its presence throws weight onto the disciples specifically: these very men, worn out from the mission they've just completed. "Apart" is kat' idian, the language of privacy — what they need is escape from the crowd pressing on them, not simply rest in the abstract. "Desert place" is erēmos, meaning uninhabited, not sandy — any quiet, unpopulated spot would serve. Jesus is as careful of His workers' need for recovery as He is of anyone's need for ministry; He takes His own rest seriously enough to insist His disciples take theirs too. But the crowd outruns the boat, converging from every town along the shore faster than a small vessel can outpace a determined crowd circling the lake on foot — proof of how little privacy this particular deserted place was about to offer.
translation: And he said to them, Come, you yourselves, apart into a deserted place by yourselves, and rest a while. For those coming and going were many, and they did not even have opportunity to eat.

label: Mark 6:34
text: The construction behind "began to teach" marks continuous, ongoing action — Jesus doesn't merely start teaching, He keeps at it hour after hour, despite having come ashore looking for exactly the rest this crowd is now denying Him. "Moved with compassion" is one of the rare places where the traditional English earns its keep — it captures a gut-level, visceral response to a crowd Jesus sees as sheep without a shepherd, unprotected and without direction. By the time evening presses in and the disciples suggest sending everyone off to the surrounding farms and villages to buy food, the day has been running for hours on nothing but that compassion.
translation: And coming out, he saw a great crowd, and he was moved in his inward parts with compassion for them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd; and he kept on teaching them many things.

label: Mark 6:37
text: "Give ye them to eat" throws heavy emphasis onto "ye" — as for you, you feed them — a pointed challenge to disciples who have just spent a whole tour exercising delegated authority over demons and disease, and are now stumped by a logistics problem. Their reply calculates the cost in denarii, the standard day's wage: roughly two hundred days' pay, a figure probably named because it was close to what the Twelve actually had between them — offered less as a genuine plan than as proof of how impossible the request sounded to them.
translation: But he answered and said to them, As for you, you give them something to eat. And they say to him, Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?

label: Mark 6:38
text: The command to have the crowd "sit down" uses anaklinō, the verb for reclining at a banquet table, not simply taking a seat — the crowd is arranged as if for a formal meal, propped on one elbow on the grass the way a guest would recline on a couch. "By companies" translates a Greek idiom formed by doubling the word for a dinner-party — group by group, table-party by table-party — and "in ranks" doubles the word for a garden bed — plot by plot. Set side by side, the two phrases paint one picture: block after block of people in their bright, ordinary clothing, arranged across the green Passover-season grass so that it looked, from a distance, like a field broken into flowerbeds.
translation: And he commanded them all to recline, group by group, table-party by table-party, upon the green grass. And they reclined in groups, plot by plot, by hundreds, and by fifties.

label: Mark 6:41
text: "Brake" and "gave" sit in two different tenses in the Greek — the breaking is aorist, a single decisive act, while the giving is imperfect, a continuous, repeated action unfolding again and again. The multiplication itself seems to have happened in that gap: not in one dramatic flash, but somewhere in the ongoing motion of Jesus's hands passing bread to the disciples repeatedly, more coming each time than the last handful could have accounted for.
translation: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves, and kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all.

label: Mark 6:42–44
text: "Basket" is kophinos, the wicker hand-basket a Jewish traveler typically carried — a small, personal container, not a hamper. "Five thousand men" uses anēr, the word specifically for adult males, not the generic term that would include women and children — meaning the actual crowd fed that day was considerably larger than the headline number suggests.
translation: And they all ate and were filled. And they took up twelve small wicker baskets full of fragments, and also of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand adult men.

label: Mark 6:45
text: Jesus "compels" His disciples onto the boat — a stronger word than merely asking them to go — while He stays behind to dismiss the crowd Himself, sending the Twelve on ahead across the lake toward Bethsaida rather than have them wait on Him. Whatever charged mood the crowd had worked itself into by then, Jesus wanted His disciples clear of it before He dealt with it alone.
translation: And immediately he compelled his disciples to get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he himself was dismissing the crowd.

label: Mark 6:46
text: "Sent them away" is apotassō, a verb of formal leave-taking, a deliberate goodbye rather than a casual dismissal. "To pray" is proseuchomai, built on a preposition meaning "toward" or "facing" — prayer conceived as a direct approach into Someone's presence, not words simply spoken into the air. Jesus goes up the mountain alone, consciously seeking His Father's face after a day that had cost Him everything He had to give.
translation: And having said farewell to them, he went off into the mountain to pray, facing toward God.

label: Mark 6:47
text: Evening has fully come — the later of the two evenings the Jewish day recognized, somewhere around sunset — and the picture the verse leaves is a stark one: the disciples are out in the middle of the lake, and Jesus is entirely alone on the shore, having apparently stayed on the beach for hours after leaving the mountain, still praying, still waiting.
translation: And when evening had come, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land.

label: Mark 6:48
text: "Toiling in rowing" translates basanizō, a word that elsewhere means "to torture" — the disciples aren't merely working hard at the oars, they're being tormented by a headwind that won't let up. "Walking on the sea" uses a preposition of contact: His feet are actually touching the water's surface, the way ours touch pavement. And the phrase usually rendered "would have passed by them" is better read the other way — verb and preposition together mean "to come alongside," not "to go past": Jesus is heading out into that wind to reach them, not to walk by and leave them to it.
translation: And seeing them being continually tormented in their rowing, for the wind was against them, about the fourth watch of the night he comes toward them, walking upon the sea, and he was wishing to come alongside them.

label: Mark 6:49
text: The word for what the disciples think they're seeing is phantasma, not the ordinary word for a departed spirit — phantasma carries associations of magic and sorcery, an apparition conjured up rather than a ghost returned. A man walking on water read to them as witchcraft, not as a soul come back from the dead. "Cried out" is a guttural verb, the kind used for a scream torn straight from the throat — sheer, wordless terror.
translation: But they, seeing him walking upon the sea, supposed that it was an apparition, a thing conjured up, and they cried out with a scream torn from the throat.

label: Mark 6:50
text: "Were afraid" translates tarassō, inward agitation, the mind thrown into turmoil rather than simple fright. "Be of good cheer" is tharseō, courage summoned in the face of danger. "It is I" carries an emphatic pronoun in the Greek — not just "it's me" but "it is I, and no one else." And "be not afraid" uses a present-tense prohibition, the grammar for stopping an action already underway: not "don't start being afraid" but "stop being afraid" — they already were.
translation: For they all saw him and were thrown into inward turmoil. And immediately he spoke with them, and says to them, Take courage; it is I myself; stop being afraid.

label: Mark 6:51
text: "Ceased" translates kopazō, a verb that pictures the wind growing weary and giving out — the storm doesn't so much stop as run out of energy, not so much halted as spent, the way a runner's stride slows on its own once the drive behind it gives out.
translation: And he went up to them into the boat, and the wind grew weary and spent itself.

label: Mark 6:52
text: "Considered not" is suniēmi, literally to put things together in the mind — to reason from one fact to the next. The disciples had just watched five loaves feed a multitude and should have reasoned from that miracle straight to this one: the same supernatural power that multiplied bread in Jesus's hands could just as easily quiet a headwind and hold a body up on open water. They didn't make the connection. "Hardened" is a perfect-tense passive, describing not a moment of dullness but a settled condition — their hearts weren't merely slow that night, they were, by that point, already callous.
translation: For they had not put together in their minds the lesson of the loaves; instead their heart had been, and remained, hardened.

label: Mark 6:53
text: "Drew to the shore" is a nautical term for bringing a vessel to its moorings — anchoring, not simply beaching it, which suggests a boat too substantial to run straight up onto the sand. "Knew him" uses a verb for recognition built on prior acquaintance — these were people who had seen Jesus before and knew exactly who was stepping off that boat. What follows is frantic: crowds running the whole circuit of the region, carrying their sick from place to place on pallets, chasing down every report of where He'd gone next — an imperfect tense picturing this scrambling search going on continuously, town after town.
translation: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and drew the boat to its moorings. And when they had come out of the boat, immediately the people, recognizing him, kept running about that whole region, and began to carry those who were sick on their pallets to wherever they heard he was.

label: Mark 6:56
text: "Border" is kraspedon, the tassel or fringe Jewish law required on the corner of a man's outer garment, meant as a standing visual reminder of the commandments — the same fringe a woman with a chronic hemorrhage had already reached for earlier in this Gospel. Here whole crowds beg simply to touch it, not because there was anything magical in the cloth itself, but because it was the nearest edge of Him they could reach — and everyone who touched it was healed.
translation: And wherever he entered, into villages, or cities, or the countryside, they kept laying the sick in the marketplaces, and kept begging him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched it were made whole.

label: Mark 7:2
text: "Defiled" translates koinos, a word that simply meant "common" — shared by everybody — before it narrowed in later Greek to mean profane, the opposite of what is set apart as sacred. Applied to hands, it meant ceremonially unclean, not physically dirty; the disciples weren't accused of poor hygiene but of skipping a ritual. The "bread" in the Greek is plural and carries the definite article — the loaves, specific ones the Pharisees and Jesus both had in mind, almost certainly leftovers from the feeding of the five thousand still sitting in the baskets. There had been no real opportunity to wash; the Pharisees weren't concerned with that, only with the broken ritual.
translation: And seeing some of his disciples eating the loaves with common, that is, unwashed, hands, they found fault.

label: Mark 7:3
text: "Oft" is actually pugmē, "with the fist" — the verb is middle voice, meaning the Pharisees washed their own hands rather than delegating it to a servant, scrubbing one closed fist against the palm and up the forearm of the other hand to be sure everything that might touch food was ritually clean. "Tradition" is paradosis, built on the verb "to hand over, to deliver into someone's keeping" — instructions passed down and expected to be kept by each new generation. "Holding" translates krateō, which carries the sense of a tight, deliberate grip, not casual observance. And "the elders" here doesn't mean the aged in general but a specific class — men of rank, originally drawn from the Sanhedrin — whose oral rulings had, by this point, taken on an authority the Pharisees treated as equal to Scripture.
translation: For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, except they wash their hands with the fist, do not eat, holding fast, with a tight grip, the tradition handed down from the elders.

label: Mark 7:4
text: The "market" is the agora, the public square where a town's business and gossip both happened — contact with the crowd there was assumed to leave a Jew ceremonially defiled, hence the washing before eating. Two different verbs sit behind the single English word "wash" in this passage: niptō, ordinary washing of hands, and baptizō, full immersion, used here of dipping cups and vessels. The "pots" are xestēs, a term borrowed from the Latin sextarius, a pint measure — a small detail that shows how deep into the specifics of daily life this scribal system reached, regulating not just people but the exact vessels they ate and drank from.
translation: And coming from the marketplace, except they immerse themselves, they do not eat. And there are many other things which they have received to hold fast: the immersing of cups, and pitchers, and bronze vessels, and couches.

label: Mark 7:5
text: Verses 3 and 4 are Mark's own explanatory aside for readers unfamiliar with Jewish custom; verse 5 picks the story back up exactly where verse 2 left off, with the Pharisees and scribes voicing the complaint out loud. Their question is pointed: not "why don't your disciples wash" but "why don't they live according to what has been handed down" — the tradition itself, not hygiene, is the real issue being pressed.
translation: Then the Pharisees and the scribes ask him, Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition handed down by the elders, but eat bread with unwashed, common hands?

label: Mark 7:6
text: "Well" is kalōs, "excellently, finely" — the same word Jesus reaches for again in verse 9, but there it turns to open sarcasm; here it's a straight compliment to Isaiah's accuracy. "Hypocrites" comes from hupokritēs, built on "to judge" with the prefix "under" — originally the word for a stage actor, someone who performed from behind a mask, playing a part rather than being it. "As it is written" renders a perfect tense: not merely "was written once" but "stands written, and stands on the record still." And the phrase "is far from me" uses a verb built from "to hold" plus "away from" — the heart isn't passively distant here, it's actively holding itself off, at a chosen remove.
translation: And he said to them, Isaiah excellently prophesied concerning you hypocrites, stage-players behind a mask, as it stands written, and stands written still: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart keeps itself held off, far away from me.

label: Mark 7:7
text: "In vain" is matēn, "fruitlessly" — the failure isn't in the sincerity of the worship but in what it accomplishes; effort spent on the wrong object produces nothing, however earnest it feels. "Worship" itself, sebomai, is a strong word, carrying real reverence and awe — Isaiah isn't accusing this people of insincerity, only of misdirection. "Doctrines" and "commandments" are both words for formal, authoritative teaching — precepts handed down and enjoined as binding — which is exactly the problem: human rulings dressed in the authority that belongs only to God's word.
translation: But fruitlessly do they worship me, teaching as their teachings the commandments of men.

label: Mark 7:8
text: "Laying aside" translates aphiēmi, a word used elsewhere of a speaker or writer setting a subject down in order to move on to something else — deliberately leaving it behind, done with. That's the picture: the Pharisees haven't merely neglected God's commandment, they've set it aside on purpose to make room for something else. That something else they "hold" — krateō again, the same tight grip from verse 3 — showing where their real zeal actually lay. The irony is exact: total abandonment of the divine command, matched by white-knuckled devotion to the human one.
translation: Leaving behind, and done with, the commandment of God, you hold fast, with a tight grip, the tradition of men.

label: Mark 7:9
text: "Full well" repeats kalōs from verse 6, but the tone has flipped into open sarcasm — "beautifully" doing bitter work here. "Reject" is atheteō, built from the word for something formally "laid down" or enacted, with a prefix that negates it — literally "to un-lay," to strip a decree of its force. It's the vocabulary of nullification, not mere disagreement: Jesus isn't saying the Pharisees dislike God's commandment, he's saying their system actively voids it, cancels its effect, so their own tradition can stand in its place.
translation: And he kept saying to them, Beautifully do you nullify, and strip of its force, the commandment of God, that you may keep your own tradition.

label: Mark 7:10
text: "Honour" is timaō, related to timē, "a valuation, a price" — to honor a parent is to assess them at their true worth and treat them accordingly, not simply to be polite. "Curseth" is a weaker word than it sounds — kakologeō, "to speak evil of, to revile" — ongoing verbal contempt, not the invoking of a divine curse, which is a different word entirely elsewhere in the New Testament. "Let him die the death" is emphatic idiom carried straight into Greek: come to his end by death — the full weight of the Mosaic penalty, reserved for habitual, unrepentant abuse, not a single sharp word spoken in anger.
translation: For Moses said, Honor your father and your mother, valuing them at their true worth; and, Whoever speaks evil of father or mother, let him come to his end by death.

label: Mark 7:11-13
text: "Corban" is a transliterated Hebrew term Mark bothers to explain for his Gentile readers — a formal designation of something as a gift devoted to God. The scribal loophole was simple: a son could declare the money owed to his aging parents "Corban," and by that one word of dedication keep it for himself while looking pious rather than negligent — technically unable to give it away now that it belonged to God, in practice free to spend it however he liked. "Making of none effect" is akuroō, "to strip of legal force" — the same root idea as verse 9's atheteō, but sharper, almost a legal term: the tradition doesn't just override God's command, it invalidates it. And "tradition" and "delivered" share the same root verb, "to hand over" — the Pharisees weren't only receiving this system, they were actively passing it on, adding their own weight to its authority with each transmission.
translation: But you say, If a man says to his father or mother, Whatever you might have been profited by me is Corban, that is to say, given to God — you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or his mother, stripping the word of God of its force by your tradition, which you have handed over, and go on handing over.

label: Mark 7:14
text: Jesus "calls the people to him again" — until now the crowd seems to have hung back respectfully while the religious leaders pressed their case, but Jesus deliberately brings them back into the conversation. He isn't finished with a private theological dispute; he wants the ordinary people to see plainly what their teachers' hair-splitting actually amounts to.
translation: And calling the crowd to himself again, he kept saying to them, Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

label: Mark 7:15
text: "Defile" is koinoō, the verb form of the koinos from verse 2 — "to make common, to profane." Jesus draws the line exactly opposite to where the Pharisees drew it: what a man eats, even with unwashed hands, cannot touch what he is on the inside — food travels one direction, through the body and out again, external to internal never crossing the line that actually matters. What comes from within — a man's own thoughts and choices — is the only thing capable of making him common, unholy, unfit.
translation: There is nothing outside a man which, going into him, is able to make him common; but the things coming out from within a man are the things that make the man common.

label: Mark 7:16
text: This verse doesn't appear in the earliest manuscripts behind the modern critical text. It reads like a later addition, echoing the refrain from 4:9 and 4:23 to round the saying off, rather than something Mark originally wrote here.
translation: If any man has ears to hear, let him keep on hearing.

label: Mark 7:17-19
text: The disciples' question comes fast — the verb is an inceptive imperfect, "they began asking," fired off the moment they were alone with him in the house, before the crowd's dust had even settled. Jesus' reply is pointed: "are you also without understanding" groups the Twelve with the very crowd they'd just left behind, still thinking in categories of ceremonial defilement. He spells out the mechanics almost clinically — koilia, the stomach and bowels, is where food goes, and the word behind "draught" was plain classical Greek for a latrine; none of that route passes through the heart, which is the only place real defilement could register. Many take the aside "thus purging all meats" to be Mark's own editorial comment rather than Jesus' spoken words — his explanation, in hindsight, of where this teaching was heading: the abolition of the whole clean/unclean food system, the very point Peter would later need a rooftop vision to fully absorb.
translation: And when he had entered the house, away from the crowd, his disciples began asking him about the parable. And he says to them, Are even you also still without understanding? Do you not perceive that whatever from outside enters into a man is not able to make him common, because it does not enter into his heart, but into the stomach and bowels, and goes out into the latrine? Thus he declared all foods clean.

label: Mark 7:20-23
text: "Evil thoughts" pairs a word carrying an undertone of internal debate or suspicion with kakos, "wickedness" in its most basic, almost neutral sense — simply not what it ought to be. The list that follows shifts to a stronger word, ponēria, wickedness actively engaged, and the difference matters: a kakos man is content to ruin himself; a ponēros man isn't satisfied until he's dragged others down with him. "Lasciviousness" is aselgeia, broader than mere sexual excess — a general contempt for restraint, insolence that no longer bothers to hide itself. The "evil eye" is a single phrase for a deliberately malicious, mischief-working glance, and "pride" is built from "to show oneself above" — the picture of a man holding his head literally higher than the people around him. Stacking up thirteen items this way, Jesus makes a cumulative point: none of it arrives from outside a man and lodges in him; all of it was already native to the heart, merely waiting for occasion.
translation: And he kept saying, That which comes out of the man, that is what makes the man common. For from within, out of the heart of men, evil reasonings keep coming out: fornications, thefts, murders, adulteries, covetous desires, wicked schemes, deceit, unrestrained excess, a mischief-working eye, slander, a lifting of oneself above others, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and keep making the man common.

label: Mark 7:24
text: The little conjunction usually rendered "and" reads better here as adversative — "but" — marking a real turn in the story: Jesus leaves Jewish Galilee, where he's just clashed with the religious leadership, and crosses into pagan Phoenicia. The preposition behind "into the borders of Tyre" doesn't mean he merely stepped over a boundary line; it signals real depth of entry, well into the heart of the region, not a quick visit to its edge. He wanted privacy there, rest after a punishing stretch of ministry and conflict — and didn't get it.
translation: But rising up from there, he went off into the region of Tyre, entering deep into it; and going into a house, he wanted no one to know it, and he was not able to escape notice.

label: Mark 7:25
text: "Immediately" doesn't mean the woman heard about Jesus the instant he crossed into the country — it means that as soon as word reached her, she wasted no time getting to him. Mark's word for her daughter is a diminutive, "little daughter" — a small, affectionate touch that colors the whole scene with a mother's urgency before a word of dialogue is even spoken.
translation: But immediately a woman, whose little daughter had an unclean spirit, hearing about him, came and fell down at his feet.

label: Mark 7:26
text: Mark stacks up three separate identifiers for this woman — Greek by religion (meaning simply Gentile, not ethnically Greek), Syrian by language, Phoenician by race — making sure no reader mistakes her for anything but a complete outsider to Israel's covenant. "Besought" is an imperfect tense, describing not a single request but a woman who kept on asking, refusing to let the conversation end; the verb itself carries the sense of an urgent appeal rather than a passing question. "Cast out," by contrast, is an aorist infinitive — she wanted the thing done decisively, in one stroke, not as a process.
translation: Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race; and she kept begging him earnestly that he would cast the demon out of her daughter, once and for all, decisively.

label: Mark 7:27
text: The everyday Greek word for "dog" — the term Jews commonly used with contempt for Gentiles — is not the word Jesus uses here. He chooses kunarion, "little dog," the diminutive: a household pet under the table, not a scavenger in the street. The distinction matters: Jesus isn't insulting her, he's stating an order of operations — his mission was first to Israel, and only through that chosen channel out to the nations — using the gentlest version of a harsh cultural metaphor to make the point without the sting it would otherwise carry.
translation: And he kept saying to her, Let the children first be filled, for it is not proper to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs under the table.

label: Mark 7:28
text: The woman answers in kind, picking up his own diminutives and adding more of her own — little dogs, little children, little crumbs — an answer built entirely out of the smallness he offered her, turned into an argument: even the little dogs under the table share what falls from the children's meal. "Lord" here is an ordinary term for master, someone with authority to dispose of a thing as he sees fit — not, on this Gentile woman's lips, a confession of Jesus' deity, simply the natural address to a man she's asking a favor of.
translation: But she answered and says to him, Yes, Master, yet even the little dogs under the table eat of the little children's little crumbs.

label: Mark 7:29
text: "For this saying" is literally "because of this word" — her answer itself, not merely her faith in the abstract, is what Jesus credits. "Is gone out" is a perfect tense: not "the demon left" as a past event only, but "the demon has gone, and stays gone" — Mark's grammar itself promises a cure that will hold.
translation: And he said to her, Because of this word, go your way; the demon has gone out of your daughter, and remains gone.

label: Mark 7:30
text: The perfect tense repeats here for the same reason — permanence, not just a past exit. And the detail of the child "laid upon the bed," resting quietly rather than thrashing or crying out, is Mark's visual confirmation of the same fact the grammar already states: this deliverance was complete, not partial or temporary.
translation: And going off to her house, she found the little child laid upon the bed, resting quietly, and the demon gone out of her, and remaining gone.

label: Mark 7:31
text: The route Mark traces is a wide loop, not a straight line — north through Sidon before doubling back southeast around the Sea of Galilee to reach Decapolis on its far shore. It's a detail worth noticing on a map: Jesus' movement here wasn't a quick detour but an extended, deliberate swing through Gentile territory before he returns to Jewish soil.
translation: And again going out from the region of Tyre, he came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the region of the Ten Cities, having made a wide circuit.

label: Mark 7:32
text: "An impediment in his speech" translates a single compound word, built from "with difficulty" and "speaking" — this man wasn't mute, he could produce sound, just not clearly. The distinction matters for what follows: Jesus doesn't give speech to someone who had none, he corrects a mechanism that was already partly working.
translation: And they bring to him a deaf man, one who could speak only with great difficulty; and they beg him to lay his hand upon him.

label: Mark 7:33
text: "Aside from the multitude" is a phrase built on the word for privacy — Jesus deliberately isolates this healing from public view, likely because he had no interest in cultivating a reputation as a wonder-worker that would crowd out his teaching. "Put his fingers into his ears" uses a verb that ordinarily means "to throw" or "thrust" — a vivid, almost forceful gesture, not a gentle touch, chosen precisely because a deaf man couldn't be spoken to and needed something physical to fix his attention and draw out his faith.
translation: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he thrust his fingers into his ears, and spitting, he touched his tongue.

label: Mark 7:34
text: "He sighed" is a word for groaning, real emotional weight rather than a formality attached to prayer — Jesus feels the burden of this man's condition even as he moves to heal it. "Ephphatha" is Aramaic, and Mark, writing for readers who wouldn't know the language, translates it on the spot: "be opened."
translation: And looking up to heaven, he groaned deeply, and says to him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened.

label: Mark 7:35
text: "His ears were opened" puts the Greek word for hearing itself as the object, not merely an anatomical part. "The string of his tongue" is literally "that which bound it," loosed the moment his hearing returned. The verb behind "spake plain" is an inchoative imperfect — "he began to be speaking" — catching the process right as it started, a man discovering mid-sentence that the words were finally coming out right.
translation: And immediately his hearing was opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he began speaking, and kept on speaking, plainly.

label: Mark 7:36
text: "He charged them" is diastellō, a verb that originally meant simply "to separate" or "mark off," and came to mean "give a strict, particular order" — used here in the middle voice, which suggests Jesus had a personal stake in the silence he was requesting, not just procedural caution. The Greek behind "so much the more" stacks two comparative words on top of each other for emphasis — the harder he pressed for silence, the louder and wider the news spread anyway.
translation: And he charged them, for his own sake, that they should tell no one; but the more he kept charging them, all the more abundantly, beyond all measure, they kept proclaiming it.

label: Mark 7:37
text: "Beyond measure astonished" likewise stacks two intensifying words, "superabundantly" plus "above" — description straining at its own limits to capture a crowd nearly knocked out of their composure. The verb behind their reaction, in fact, originally meant exactly that: to strike someone out of their senses. "He hath done all things well" is a perfect tense — not a passing impression but a settled verdict the crowd has arrived at and isn't backing away from.
translation: And they were astonished, superabundantly, beyond all measure, struck clean out of their senses, saying, He has done, and stands having done, all things well; he even makes the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.

label: Mark 8:4
text:
The disciples' question, “From whence?” translates *pothen* (πόθεν), an adverb regularly used of the source of a food supply — closer to “how could anyone manage to…” than a plain “from where.” Their word for “satisfy,” *chortazō* (χορτάζω), is telling: in ordinary Greek usage it was the word for filling livestock with fodder — hay, grass, feed — and only later got stretched, sometimes with a faint sneer, to cover filling human stomachs. The disciples are thinking in barnyard terms: how do you fill this many mouths out here? “The wilderness” is *erēmia* (ἐρημία), an uninhabited waste with no markets and no houses — and remarkably, this is the second time Jesus has faced this exact problem with a crowd this size; the memory of the five thousand seems to have evaporated completely.

The Greek of the verses that follow also carries a nuance English flattens out. Jesus “kept giving” the broken bread to the disciples so that they “might keep on setting it forth” — continuous, repeated action, not a single hand-off but an ongoing relay between His hands and theirs as the crowd was fed.
translation: And his disciples answered him, From where will anyone be able here, in this wasteland with no houses, to fill these people with bread, as one fills cattle with fodder? And he kept giving the loaves to his disciples so that they might keep on setting them before the people.

label: Mark 8:7
text:
When Jesus “blessed” the small fish (*eulogeō*, εὐλογέω), He was doing what any Jew did over a meal — asking God to set His blessing on the food for its intended use. Grace before meals traces straight back to this moment. The “broken pieces” left over are *klasma* (κλάσμα), a word for substantial remnants rather than crumbs — these were sizable leftover portions, not scraps swept off the table. (The KJV's “meat” here simply meant “food” in 1611 English and isn't in the Greek at all; the translators supplied it to smooth the sentence.)

The location, Dalmanutha, is otherwise unknown, but the region was Decapolis — Gentile territory the Pharisees normally avoided as unclean. That they crossed into it to confront Jesus signals how determined the opposition had become. “Began to question” renders a present-tense verb of continuous action built on *sunzēteō* (συνζητέω), “to examine together, to dispute” — not a single query but a running interrogation that escalated into open argument, with Jesus Himself grammatically marked as an active party rather than merely a target. Their demand was for a *sēmeion* (σημεῖον), a “sign” understood as a certifying credential — proof that the one performing it truly spoke for God. And “tempting” Him is *peirazomai* (πειράζομαι), a word whose root sense is neutral testing — putting something to the proof to see what's really there — before it darkened elsewhere into “tempting to evil.” Here it keeps the neutral sense: they were testing whether His claims held up, not baiting Him to sin.
translation: And he also blessed the few small fish, asking God's blessing upon them. And they took up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven large baskets full. And the Pharisees came out and began to dispute with him, examining the matter together with him, seeking from him a sign, a certifying proof from heaven, putting him to the test.

label: Mark 8:12
text:
“He sighed deeply in His spirit” intensifies a simple verb for groaning (*stenazō*, στενάζω) with a prefix that pushes it further — not a passing sigh but a groan from the depths, His inner being visibly disturbed. There's real reason for it: this isn't the flat unbelief of an ordinary skeptic but calculated hostility from men who had watched Him work miracles and had already begun explaining them away as demonic. The refusal that follows, “there shall no sign be given,” is built on a Hebrew oath formula — literally “if a sign shall be given,” the truncated form of a self-curse (“may such-and-such happen to me if…”).
